topics.title: Application
topics.summary: The Rules apply to all vessels on the high seas and in all waters connected to them that seagoing vessels can navigate. Local authorities may make special rules for harbours, rivers and inland waters, but those rules must follow the COLREGs as closely as possible.
points: Covers every vessel, from a dinghy to a VLCC, on the high seas and connected navigable waters.
Local rules for roadsteads, harbours, rivers, lakes and inland waterways take precedence there, but must conform as closely as possible.
Governments may allow extra station or signal lights, shapes or whistle signals for warships, convoys and fishing fleets.
IMO may adopt traffic separation schemes for the purpose of these Rules.
Vessels of special construction or purpose comply as closely as possible, as their Government decides.

ask.q: You are bound for a river port with its own local regulations. Which rules apply?
ask.a: The local rules apply within their limits; the COLREGs apply wherever the local rules are silent. Check Sailing Directions and the port's regulations during passage planning.

ask.q: Who adopts traffic separation schemes for the purpose of the Rules?
ask.a: IMO (Rule 1(d)).

check.q: Where do the COLREGs apply?
options: On the high seas and connected waters navigable by seagoing vessels
check.why: Rule 1(a): the high seas and all waters connected to them that are navigable by seagoing vessels.

topics.title: Responsibility
topics.summary: Following the Rules does not excuse neglect of ordinary good seamanship. In special circumstances, including the limitations of the vessels involved, you may have to depart from the Rules to avoid immediate danger.
points: Owner, Master and crew stay responsible for the consequences of neglecting the Rules or ordinary seamanship.
You must allow for all dangers of navigation and collision and any special circumstances.
Departure from the Rules is allowed only when necessary to avoid immediate danger.
Rule 2 is the 'good seamanship' rule; it is never a licence to ignore the steering rules early in an encounter.

ask.q: When may you depart from the Rules?
ask.a: Only when special circumstances, including the limitations of the vessels involved, make it necessary to avoid immediate danger (Rule 2(b)).

ask.q: Give an example of 'ordinary practice of seamen'.
ask.a: Examples: calling the Master early, reducing speed in heavy traffic, giving a wide berth to a vessel at anchor, keeping clear of a fishing fleet, posting an extra lookout in fog.

check.q: Rule 2(b) permits departure from the Rules when:
options: It is necessary to avoid immediate danger
The other vessel agrees on VHF
check.why: Departure is permitted only to avoid immediate danger, having regard to special circumstances.

topics.title: General definitions
topics.summary: Rule 3 defines the terms the rest of the Rules depend on: vessel, power-driven vessel, sailing vessel, engaged in fishing, not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught, underway, in sight and restricted visibility.
points: Sailing vessel: under sail, provided any propelling machinery is not being used.
Engaged in fishing: using nets, lines, trawls or other gear that restricts manoeuvrability. Trolling lines do not count.
Not under command: unable to manoeuvre as the Rules require through some exceptional circumstance.

Restricted in ability to manoeuvre: limited by the nature of her work. Examples: buoy, cable or pipeline work; dredging, surveying or underwater operations; replenishment or transfer under way; launching or recovering aircraft; mine clearance; a restrictive tow.
Constrained by draught: a power-driven vessel severely restricted in deviating from her course by her draught in relation to the available depth and width of water.
Underway: not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground. In sight: only when one can be observed visually from the other.
Restricted visibility: fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rainstorms, sandstorms or any similar cause.

ask.q: A ship drifting with her engine stopped and no breakdown: is she underway, and is she making way?
ask.a: She is underway (not anchored, made fast or aground) but not making way through the water.

ask.q: Is a ship with a main engine failure RAM or NUC?
ask.a: NUC: an exceptional circumstance. RAM comes from the nature of her work.

check.q: Which vessel is 'restricted in her ability to manoeuvre'?
options: A vessel with a steering gear failure
A vessel laying a submarine cable
A deep-draught tanker in a channel
check.why: Cable laying is listed in Rule 3(g). Steering failure is NUC, the trawler is engaged in fishing, the tanker may be constrained by draught.

topics.title: Application of Section I
topics.summary: Rules 4 to 10 apply in any condition of visibility: clear, restricted, by day or by night.
points: Look-out, safe speed, risk of collision, action to avoid collision, narrow channels and TSS rules apply whether or not vessels are in sight of one another.

ask.q: Does Rule 8 apply in fog?
ask.a: Yes. Section I (Rules 4 to 10) applies in any condition of visibility, so Rule 8 applies alongside Rule 19.

check.q: Section I of Part B applies:
options: Only when vessels are in sight
check.why: Rule 4: Rules 4 to 10 apply in any condition of visibility.

topics.title: Look-out
topics.summary: Every vessel must keep a proper look-out at all times, by sight and hearing and by all available means, so as to make a full appraisal of the situation and the risk of collision.
points: 'All available means' includes radar, ARPA, AIS and VHF, but never replaces sight and hearing.
The look-out must be able to give full attention to that task.
STCW A-VIII/2: the OOW may be the sole look-out only in daylight, after careful assessment, with assistance immediately available.
Many collisions are traced back to a poor look-out more than any other single rule.

ask.q: When can the OOW be the sole look-out?
ask.a: Only in daylight, after the situation has been carefully assessed and found safe (weather, visibility, traffic, hazards, TSS), and with help immediately available if needed.

ask.q: Is AIS an 'available means'? What are its limits?
ask.a: Yes, but not every vessel carries or transmits AIS, data can be wrong or delayed, and it must not replace visual and radar look-out.

check.q: A proper look-out is kept by:
options: Sight and hearing and all available means
check.why: Rule 5: sight and hearing as well as all available means appropriate to the circumstances.

topics.title: Safe speed
topics.summary: Every vessel must proceed at a safe speed at all times, so that she can take proper and effective action to avoid collision and stop within a distance appropriate to the circumstances.
points: Factors for all vessels: visibility; traffic density, including fishing fleets; manoeuvrability, especially stopping distance and turning ability; background light at night; wind, sea and current and nearby hazards; draught against available depth.

Extra factors with radar: its characteristics and limits; range scale in use; sea state, weather and interference; small craft, ice and floating objects it may miss; the number, position and movement of targets; the better estimate of visibility radar can give.
There is no fixed number: safe speed is a judgement and can change minute by minute.
In fog, Rule 19(b) adds that engines must be ready for immediate manoeuvre.

ask.q: What would you consider when setting a safe speed in fog in a busy approach?
ask.a: Visibility, traffic density, stopping distance and turning circle, sea state, UKC and hazards, radar performance and clutter, small targets radar may miss, and engines on standby (Rule 6 and 19(b)).

ask.q: Does safe speed mean slow speed?
ask.a: Not always. It is the speed that lets you act effectively and stop in time. In some cases keeping steerage way and manoeuvrability matters more.

check.q: Which is a factor for ALL vessels under Rule 6(a)?
options: Number of targets detected by radar
check.why: Background light is in Rule 6(a). The others are radar factors in Rule 6(b).

topics.title: Risk of collision
topics.summary: Use all available means to decide whether risk of collision exists. If in doubt, assume it does. Radar must be used properly, and no assumption may be made on scanty information.
points: Risk exists if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change.
Risk may still exist with an appreciable bearing change, especially with a very large vessel, a tow, or at close range.
Proper radar use includes long-range scanning for early warning and radar plotting or equivalent systematic observation (ARPA).
Do not decide on scanty information, especially scanty radar information.

ask.q: Why a compass bearing rather than a relative bearing?
ask.a: A relative bearing changes with own ship's yaw or heading change; a compass bearing reflects the true geometry.

ask.q: The bearing of a large tanker is changing slowly at 2 nm. Is there risk?
ask.a: Possibly. With a large vessel, a tow or at close range, risk may exist even with an appreciable bearing change (Rule 7(d)(ii)). Check CPA and TCPA on ARPA.

check.q: If you are in doubt about risk of collision you should:
options: Call the other vessel on VHF and wait
check.why: Rule 7(a): if there is any doubt, such risk shall be deemed to exist.

topics.title: Action to avoid collision
topics.summary: Action must be positive, taken in ample time and in line with good seamanship. Alterations must be large enough to be readily apparent, and the result must be checked until the other vessel is finally past and clear.
points: Avoid a series of small alterations of course or speed.
With enough sea room, a course alteration alone may be most effective, if made early, substantial and does not create another close-quarters situation.
Pass at a safe distance and keep checking the effectiveness of the action until finally past and clear.
If necessary, slacken speed or take all way off by stopping or reversing.
8(f): a vessel required not to impede must act early to leave sea room. That duty remains even if risk of collision develops, and the other vessel still has to follow the steering rules.

ask.q: What does 'readily apparent' mean in practice?
ask.a: Large enough that the other vessel sees it visually or on radar: typically 30 degrees or more, or a major speed reduction, not 5 or 10 degree nibbles.

ask.q: A small vessel must not impede you, but she is now on a collision course. Who acts?
ask.a: Both may need to. She still has her duty not to impede, and you must follow the steering and sailing rules as risk of collision now exists (Rule 8(f)(ii) and (iii)).

check.q: Under Rule 8, action to avoid collision should be:
options: A series of small alterations to avoid alarming the other vessel
Positive, in ample time and large enough to be readily apparent
Delayed until the CPA is under 0.5 nm

topics.title: Narrow channels
topics.summary: Keep as near to the outer limit of the channel on your starboard side as is safe and practicable. Small, sailing and fishing vessels must not impede vessels that can only navigate within the channel.
points: Vessels under 20 m and sailing vessels must not impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within the channel.
Fishing vessels must not impede any other vessel navigating within the channel.
Do not cross the channel if that impedes a vessel that can only navigate within it. She may sound five short blasts if in doubt.
Overtaking where the overtaken vessel must act: two prolonged + one short (your starboard side) or two prolonged + two short (your port side). Agreement: prolonged, short, prolonged, short.
Approaching a bend or obstruction: one prolonged blast, answered by one prolonged blast.
Avoid anchoring in a narrow channel if circumstances admit.

ask.q: Give the overtaking signals in a narrow channel.
ask.a: Two prolonged then one short: I intend to overtake you on your starboard side. Two prolonged then two short: on your port side. Agreement: one prolonged, one short, one prolonged, one short (Rule 34(c)).

ask.q: Does agreement to be overtaken change Rule 13?
ask.a: No. The overtaking vessel still keeps out of the way (Rule 9(e)(ii)).

check.q: In a narrow channel a vessel under 20 m shall:
options: Not impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within the channel
Have right of way over larger vessels
Anchor if the channel is busy

topics.title: Traffic separation schemes
topics.summary: Rule 10 governs schemes adopted by IMO. It does not relieve any vessel of her obligations under the other Rules. Use the correct lane in the direction of traffic flow, and cross lanes as nearly at right angles as practicable.
points: Proceed in the appropriate lane in the general direction of traffic flow, clear of the separation line or zone.
Join or leave at the end of a lane; from the side, at as small an angle as practicable.
Avoid crossing lanes; if you must, cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the traffic flow.

Inshore traffic zones: not for through traffic that can safely use the adjacent lane. Vessels under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels may use them, as may vessels bound to or from a port, offshore installation or pilot station within the zone, or avoiding immediate danger.
Fishing vessels must not impede vessels following a lane. Vessels under 20 m and sailing vessels must not impede power-driven vessels following a lane.
Avoid anchoring in a TSS or near its terminations. Vessels not using a scheme should avoid it by as wide a margin as practicable.

ask.q: Why cross on a heading at right angles rather than a track at right angles?
ask.a: A heading at right angles presents a clear aspect to vessels in the lane and minimises time in the lane, whatever the tidal set.

ask.q: Does a vessel following a lane become the stand-on vessel for crossing traffic?
ask.a: No. Rule 10 does not change the steering and sailing rules (Rule 10(a)), except the 'not impede' duties of small, sailing and fishing vessels.

check.q: When obliged to cross a traffic lane you should cross:
options: On a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of traffic flow
On a track at right angles to the separation zone

topics.title: Application of Section II
topics.summary: Rules 11 to 18 apply only to vessels in sight of one another.
points: 'In sight' means one vessel can be observed visually from the other (Rule 3(k)).
A radar-only contact in fog is not 'in sight': Rule 19 applies, and there is no stand-on or give-way vessel.

ask.q: You see a target on radar in fog, then she appears visually at 1 nm. Which rules apply from that moment?
ask.a: Once in sight, the Section II steering and sailing rules (11 to 18) apply, alongside Section I.

check.q: Rules 11 to 18 apply:
options: Only to vessels in sight of one another

topics.title: Sailing vessels
topics.summary: Between two sailing vessels: on different tacks, the port-tack vessel keeps clear; on the same tack, the windward vessel keeps clear. A port-tack vessel unsure of the other's tack keeps clear.
points: Windward side: the side opposite to that on which the mainsail is carried (largest fore-and-aft sail for a square-rigger).
Port tack: wind coming over the port side, mainsail out to starboard.
If a port-tack vessel sees a vessel to windward and cannot tell her tack, she keeps clear.

ask.q: Two yachts on the same tack converge. Which gives way?
ask.a: The windward vessel keeps out of the way of the leeward vessel (Rule 12(a)(ii)).

check.q: Two sailing vessels with the wind on different sides:

topics.title: Overtaking
topics.summary: Any vessel overtaking another keeps out of the way, whatever else Part B Sections I and II say. You are overtaking when coming up from more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam: at night you would see only her sternlight.
points: Overrides Rule 18: a sailing vessel overtaking a power-driven vessel must keep clear.
If in doubt whether you are overtaking, assume you are.
A later change in bearing does not turn it into a crossing situation; the duty lasts until finally past and clear.
The overtaken vessel is the stand-on vessel and follows Rule 17.

ask.q: A vessel on your starboard quarter, 50 degrees abaft the beam, is closing and you can see her red sidelight. Who gives way?
ask.a: She does. She is more than 22.5 degrees abaft your beam, so she is overtaking (Rule 13). You stand on (Rule 17).

ask.q: A yacht under sail is overtaking you. Who keeps clear?
ask.a: The yacht. Rule 13 applies 'notwithstanding' the other rules, and Rule 18 begins 'except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 otherwise require'.

check.q: A vessel is overtaking when she comes up from:
options: More than 22.5 degrees abaft the other vessel's beam
More than 45 degrees abaft the beam

topics.title: Head-on situation
topics.summary: Two power-driven vessels meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses, with risk of collision, each alter to starboard and pass port to port.
points: Deemed to exist when you see the other ahead or nearly ahead, by night with masthead lights in line or nearly in line and/or both sidelights, by day with the matching aspect.
If in doubt, assume it is head-on and act accordingly.
Each vessel acts; neither is stand-on.
Signal: one short blast when altering to starboard (Rule 34(a)).

ask.q: You see her masthead lights nearly in line and her red sidelight only, fine on your starboard bow. Head-on or crossing?
ask.a: If in doubt, assume head-on (Rule 14(c)). Alter to starboard boldly; one short blast.

ask.q: Does Rule 14 apply to a sailing vessel meeting a power-driven vessel?
ask.a: No. Rule 14 is for two power-driven vessels; Rule 18 applies to the sailing vessel case.

check.q: In a head-on situation between two power-driven vessels:
options: The vessel to port gives way

topics.title: Crossing situation
topics.summary: When two power-driven vessels are crossing with risk of collision, the vessel that has the other on her own starboard side keeps out of the way and, if circumstances admit, avoids crossing ahead of her.
points: 'See red, take action': if you see her port (red) sidelight on your starboard side, you give way.
Normally alter to starboard to pass astern of her; or reduce speed, stop or go astern (Rule 8(e)).
Crossing ahead of the stand-on vessel should be avoided.

ask.q: Why not alter to port to pass ahead of a crossing vessel on your starboard bow?
ask.a: Rule 15 says avoid crossing ahead if circumstances admit, and a port alteration may conflict with any late action she takes under Rule 17, which would normally be to starboard.

check.q: In a crossing situation, the give-way vessel is the one that:
options: Has the other on her own port side
Has the other on her own starboard side

topics.title: Action by give-way vessel
topics.summary: A vessel required to keep out of the way must, so far as possible, take early and substantial action to keep well clear.
points: Early: in ample time, not at close quarters.
Substantial: readily apparent to the other vessel (Rule 8(b)).
Well clear: a safe passing distance in line with company or Master's standing orders.

ask.q: What CPA would you aim for in open water?
ask.a: Whatever the Master's standing orders say, typically at least 1 to 2 nm in open sea, more for large vessels or poor conditions; the answer should cite standing orders.

check.q: Rule 16 requires the give-way vessel to take:
options: Early and substantial action to keep well clear
No action until the stand-on vessel acts

topics.title: Action by stand-on vessel
topics.summary: The stand-on vessel keeps her course and speed. She may act by her own manoeuvre once it is clear the give-way vessel is not acting, and she must act when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone.
points: 17(a)(i): keep course and speed.
17(a)(ii): may act once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action. Sound at least five short and rapid blasts first (Rule 34(d)).
17(b): must take the action that best aids avoiding collision when so close that the give-way vessel alone cannot avoid it.
17(c): a power-driven vessel acting under 17(a)(ii) in a crossing situation should not alter to port for a vessel on her own port side.
17(d): none of this relieves the give-way vessel of her obligation.

ask.q: She is on your port bow, crossing, CPA zero, and showing no sign of action at 3 nm. What do you do?
ask.a: Sound at least five short and rapid blasts, call the Master. If she still does not act, take action under 17(a)(ii): typically a bold alteration to starboard or a speed reduction, never to port for a vessel on your port side.

ask.q: Why not alter to port?
ask.a: The give-way vessel is likely to alter to starboard at the last moment; a port alteration by you would turn towards her and could cause the collision.

check.q: Under Rule 17(c), a power-driven stand-on vessel acting under 17(a)(ii) should not:
options: Alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side

topics.title: Responsibilities between vessels
topics.summary: Rule 18 sets an order of priority between types of vessel, except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 say otherwise. A power-driven vessel keeps out of the way of NUC, RAM, fishing and sailing vessels.
points: Power-driven vessel underway keeps out of the way of: NUC, RAM, a vessel engaged in fishing, a sailing vessel.
Sailing vessel keeps out of the way of: NUC, RAM, a vessel engaged in fishing.
Vessel engaged in fishing keeps out of the way, so far as possible, of: NUC, RAM.
Any vessel other than NUC or RAM avoids impeding a vessel constrained by her draught showing Rule 28 signals. The CBD vessel navigates with particular caution.
Seaplanes on the water and WIG craft taking off, landing or flying near the surface keep well clear of all vessels.
Exceptions: overtaking (Rule 13), narrow channels (Rule 9) and TSS (Rule 10).

ask.q: A sailing vessel is crossing from your port side. Who gives way?
ask.a: You do, as a power-driven vessel (Rule 18(a)). Rule 15 applies only between two power-driven vessels.

ask.q: A fishing vessel in a TSS lane is on a collision course with a power-driven vessel following the lane. What does Rule 10(i) add?
ask.a: The fishing vessel must not impede the passage of the vessel following the lane, even though Rule 18 would otherwise give the fishing vessel priority.

check.q: A sailing vessel underway must keep out of the way of:
options: A vessel constrained by draught only
check.why: Rule 18(b): NUC, RAM and vessels engaged in fishing.

topics.title: Conduct in restricted visibility
topics.summary: Applies to vessels not in sight of one another in or near an area of restricted visibility. There is no stand-on or give-way vessel. Each vessel proceeds at a safe speed and takes avoiding action in ample time based on radar.
points: Safe speed for the conditions; power-driven vessels keep engines ready for immediate manoeuvre.
A vessel detecting another by radar alone must decide whether a close-quarters situation is developing or risk exists, and act in ample time.
If altering course, avoid so far as possible: (i) altering to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than one being overtaken; (ii) altering towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.

On hearing a fog signal apparently forward of the beam, or if a close-quarters situation forward of the beam cannot be avoided: reduce to the minimum speed to keep course, take all way off if necessary, and navigate with extreme caution until the danger is over.
Rule 19 is the rule examiners press hardest; candidates often fail by talking about stand-on vessels in fog.

ask.q: In fog a target is on your port bow, closing, CPA 0.2 nm. Can you alter to port?
ask.a: Avoid it: the target is forward of the beam and not being overtaken (19(d)(i)). Alter boldly to starboard and/or reduce speed.

ask.q: A target is on your starboard quarter, closing. Which alteration should you avoid?
ask.a: Altering towards her, i.e. to starboard (19(d)(ii)). Altering to port takes you away.

ask.q: You hear a fog signal forward of the beam with nothing on radar. Action?
ask.a: Reduce to the minimum speed at which you can keep your course, take all way off if necessary, and navigate with extreme caution (19(e)). Call the Master, extra look-out.

check.q: Under Rule 19, for a vessel detected by radar alone forward of the beam (not being overtaken), you should avoid:
options: An alteration of course to port
An alteration of course to starboard

topics.title: Application of Part C
topics.summary: Lights are shown from sunset to sunrise in all weathers, and also by day in restricted visibility. Shapes are shown by day. No other lights may be shown that could be mistaken for them or impair the look-out.
points: Lights from sunset to sunrise; also from sunrise to sunset in restricted visibility, and at other times if deemed necessary.
No other lights that could be mistaken for prescribed lights, impair their visibility or distinctive character, or interfere with a proper look-out.
Shapes by day.
Technical details are in Annex I.

ask.q: Must you show navigation lights at noon in fog?
ask.a: Yes: Rule 20(c).

check.q: Navigation lights must be shown:
options: From sunset to sunrise, and also by day in restricted visibility
Only when other vessels are present

topics.title: Definitions of lights
topics.summary: Rule 21 defines each light by colour and arc: masthead 225 degrees, sidelights 112.5 degrees each, sternlight 135 degrees, towing light 135 degrees yellow, all-round 360 degrees, and flashing light at 120 or more flashes a minute.
points: Masthead light: white, fore-and-aft centreline, 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.
Sidelights: green to starboard, red to port, each 112.5 degrees from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam. Under 20 m they may be combined in one lantern.
Sternlight: white, near the stern, 135 degrees, 67.5 degrees each side of right aft.
Towing light: yellow, same characteristics as the sternlight.
All-round light: unbroken 360 degrees. Flashing light: 120 or more flashes per minute.

ask.q: Add the masthead arc and the sternlight arc. What do you get, and why does it matter?
ask.a: 225 + 135 = 360. Every aspect shows either masthead or sternlight, and the boundary at 22.5 degrees abaft the beam is the overtaking boundary in Rule 13.

check.q: The arc of a sternlight is:

topics.title: Visibility of lights
topics.summary: Minimum ranges depend on length. At 50 m or more: masthead 6 nm, sidelights 3 nm, others 3 nm. From 12 to 50 m: masthead 5 nm (3 nm under 20 m), sidelights 2 nm, others 2 nm. Under 12 m: masthead 2 nm, sidelights 1 nm, others 2 nm.
points: 50 m or more: masthead 6, sidelight 3, sternlight 3, towing 3, all-round 3 nm.
12 to 50 m: masthead 5 (3 if under 20 m), sidelight 2, sternlight 2, towing 2, all-round 2 nm.
Under 12 m: masthead 2, sidelight 1, sternlight 2, towing 2, all-round 2 nm.
Inconspicuous, partly submerged towed objects: all-round white 3 nm.

ask.q: You see sidelights at about 3 nm but no masthead light. What might that mean?
ask.a: Possibly a masthead light failure, or a sailing vessel; check by radar and AIS. A power-driven vessel of 50 m or more shows a masthead light visible at 6 nm, so you should have seen it first.

check.q: Minimum range of the masthead light of a vessel of 50 m or more:

topics.title: Power-driven vessels underway
topics.summary: A power-driven vessel underway shows a masthead light forward, a second masthead light abaft and higher (optional under 50 m), sidelights and a sternlight. Air-cushion vessels add a flashing yellow; WIG craft add a high-intensity flashing red.
points: Under 50 m the second (after) masthead light is optional.
Air-cushion vessel in non-displacement mode: add an all-round flashing yellow light.
WIG craft taking off, landing or flying near the surface: add a high-intensity all-round flashing red.
Under 12 m: may show an all-round white plus sidelights instead. Under 7 m with a top speed of 7 knots or less: all-round white, and sidelights if practicable.

ask.q: From the masthead lights alone, how can you tell which way a ship is heading?
ask.a: The forward light is lower. The direction of the higher (after) light relative to the lower shows her aspect; open masthead lights mean she is crossing, lights in line mean she is heading towards or away from you.

check.q: Under Rule 23 the second masthead light is optional for a power-driven vessel:

topics.title: Towing and pushing
topics.summary: A towing vessel shows two masthead lights in a vertical line (three if the tow is over 200 m), sidelights, a sternlight and a yellow towing light above the sternlight. With a tow over 200 m, a diamond is shown by day on the tug and on the tow.
points: Length of tow: from the stern of the towing vessel to the after end of the tow.
Towed vessel: sidelights and sternlight; a diamond if the tow exceeds 200 m.
Pushing ahead or towing alongside (not a composite unit): two masthead lights in a vertical line, sidelights, sternlight; no towing light.
A rigidly connected composite unit is lit as one power-driven vessel.
A towing vessel of 50 m or more also shows the after masthead light.
Inconspicuous, partly submerged tows: all-round white lights at the ends (and along the sides if 25 m or more wide), and a diamond at or near the after end.

ask.q: Why never pass between a tug and her tow?
ask.a: The towline may be long and low in the water, under tension or with a deep catenary; you could foul it, damage your propeller or capsize the tug.

ask.q: From astern, how do you tell a towing vessel from a pushing one?
ask.a: A towing vessel shows a yellow towing light above her sternlight; a pushing vessel shows only a sternlight.

check.q: A towing vessel whose tow exceeds 200 m shows by day:

topics.title: Sailing vessels underway and vessels under oars
topics.summary: A sailing vessel shows sidelights and a sternlight, which under 20 m may be combined in one lantern at the masthead. She may also show red over green all-round lights at the masthead, but not with the combined lantern. When also motoring by day she shows a cone, apex down.
points: No masthead light: a white masthead light means she is using her engine and counts as power-driven.
Optional all-round red over green at or near the top of the mast; not with a tricolour lantern.
Under 7 m, or under oars: if practicable the sailing lights, otherwise a white torch or lantern ready in time to prevent collision.
Motor-sailing by day: one cone, apex downwards, forward where best seen.

ask.q: You see red over green all-round lights with a green sidelight below. What is she?
ask.a: A sailing vessel underway showing her starboard side (Rule 25(c)).

check.q: A vessel under sail also using her engine shows by day:

topics.title: Fishing vessels
topics.summary: A trawler shows green over white all-round lights; other fishing vessels show red over white. By day both show two cones with apexes together. Sidelights and sternlight are added only when making way.
points: Trawling: green over white, a masthead light abaft and higher (optional under 50 m), plus sidelights and sternlight when making way.
Other fishing: red over white; gear extending over 150 m: an all-round white, or by day a cone apex up, in the direction of the gear.
Day shape for both: two cones apexes together; a basket may be used under 20 m.
Engaged in fishing, underway or at anchor, she shows only these lights and shapes (no anchor lights).
Not engaged in fishing, she shows the lights for a vessel of her length.
Annex II adds signals for fishing in close proximity.

ask.q: Memory aid for trawler versus other fishing?
ask.a: Green over white: trawling at night ('green tree'); red over white: fishing other than trawling ('red hot fishing').

ask.q: Does green over white tell you she is making way?
ask.a: No. Sidelights and sternlight show that she is making way.

check.q: A vessel engaged in fishing other than trawling shows:

topics.title: Vessels not under command or restricted in their ability to manoeuvre
topics.summary: NUC: two all-round reds, or two balls by day. RAM: red-white-red all-round, or ball-diamond-ball by day. Dredgers mark the obstructed side with two reds or two balls and the passing side with two greens or two diamonds.
points: NUC making way adds sidelights and sternlight; no masthead lights.
RAM making way adds masthead light(s), sidelights and sternlight; at anchor adds anchor lights or ball.
A towing vessel severely restricted in deviating from her course shows the RAM signals as well as the towing lights.
Dredging or underwater operations: obstruction side two all-round reds or two balls; passing side two greens or two diamonds; at anchor these replace the anchor signals.
Diving vessel too small for those signals: red-white-red at night, rigid replica of flag A at least 1 m high by day.
Mine clearance: three all-round greens or three balls (foremast head and fore-yard ends); do not approach within 1000 m.
These are not distress signals; vessels under 12 m (except diving) are not required to show them.

ask.q: Is a NUC vessel making way the stand-on vessel?
ask.a: Under Rule 18, power-driven, sailing and fishing vessels keep out of her way. She should still act if needed under Rule 17 and good seamanship.

ask.q: At anchor, does a dredger with an obstruction show an anchor ball?
ask.a: No. The Rule 27(d) signals replace the anchor signals (27(d)(iii)).

check.q: By day, a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre shows:

topics.title: Vessels constrained by their draught
topics.summary: A vessel constrained by her draught may show, in addition to power-driven vessel lights, three all-round red lights in a vertical line, or a cylinder by day.
points: It is optional ('may').
Other vessels (except NUC and RAM) must avoid impeding her if circumstances admit (Rule 18(d)).
She navigates with particular caution.
Once risk of collision exists, the steering rules apply in full (Rule 8(f)).

ask.q: Who decides that a vessel is constrained by her draught?
ask.a: The Master, considering her draught against the available depth and width of navigable water.

check.q: The day signal for a vessel constrained by her draught is:

topics.title: Pilot vessels
topics.summary: A pilot vessel on duty shows white over red all-round lights at the masthead, plus sidelights and sternlight when underway, or anchor lights when at anchor.
points: Memory aid: 'white hat, red nose'.
Off duty she shows the lights of a similar vessel of her length.
Fog: she may add an identity signal of four short blasts (Rule 35(k)).

ask.q: What is the day signal for a pilot vessel?
ask.a: The Rules give no shape; she flies flag H by day (International Code of Signals: I have a pilot on board).

check.q: A pilot vessel on duty shows at the masthead:

topics.title: Anchored vessels and vessels aground
topics.summary: At anchor: an all-round white forward and a lower one aft (one light only under 50 m), or one ball by day. Aground: anchor lights plus two all-round reds, or three balls by day.
points: At 100 m or more, deck working lights must also be used; under 100 m they may be.
Aground: anchor lights plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line; by day three balls in a vertical line.
Under 7 m at anchor clear of channels, fairways and anchorages: no lights or shape required.
Under 12 m aground: not required to show the aground lights or shapes.

ask.q: How do you tell anchor lights from masthead lights?
ask.a: Anchor lights: forward light higher, no sidelights, aspect never changes as you pass. Masthead lights: forward light lower, with sidelights.

ask.q: Two balls versus three balls?
ask.a: Two balls: not under command. Three balls in a vertical line: aground.

check.q: By day a vessel aground shows:
options: Three balls in a vertical line

topics.title: Seaplanes
topics.summary: Where a seaplane or WIG craft cannot show lights and shapes of the prescribed characteristics or positions, it shows lights and shapes as closely similar as possible.
points: Rarely examined beyond knowing the principle of closest possible compliance.

ask.q: What does Rule 18(e) require of a seaplane on the water?
ask.a: Keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding them; where risk of collision exists, follow Part B.

check.q: A seaplane that cannot show the prescribed lights shall:
options: Show lights as closely similar as possible

topics.title: Definitions (sound)
topics.summary: A short blast lasts about one second; a prolonged blast lasts four to six seconds.
points: Whistle: any sound-signalling appliance able to produce the prescribed blasts and meeting Annex III.
Short blast: about 1 s. Prolonged blast: 4 to 6 s.

ask.q: How long is a prolonged blast?
ask.a: From four to six seconds.

check.q: A prolonged blast lasts:

topics.title: Equipment for sound signals
topics.summary: Vessels of 12 m or more carry a whistle; 20 m or more also a bell; 100 m or more also a gong. Vessels under 12 m need some other means of making an efficient sound signal.
points: 12 m or more: whistle. 20 m or more: whistle and bell. 100 m or more: whistle, bell and gong.
The gong must not be confusable with the bell.
Bell and gong may be replaced by equipment with the same characteristics, provided manual sounding is always possible.

ask.q: Why does a ship of 100 m need a gong?
ask.a: At anchor or aground in fog she rings the bell forward and the gong aft, so others can judge her length and orientation (Rule 35(g)).

check.q: A vessel of 60 m must carry:

topics.title: Manoeuvring and warning signals
topics.summary: Between power-driven vessels in sight: one short blast, altering to starboard; two short, altering to port; three short, operating astern propulsion. Five or more short and rapid blasts signal doubt.
points: Light signals may supplement the whistle: one, two or three flashes of about 1 s, about 1 s apart, all-round white visible 5 nm; successive signals at least 10 s apart.
Narrow channel overtaking: two prolonged + one short (your starboard side); two prolonged + two short (your port side). Agreement: prolonged, short, prolonged, short.
Doubt or failure to understand: at least five short and rapid blasts, may be supplemented by five short rapid flashes.
Approaching a bend or obscured area: one prolonged blast; answered by one prolonged.
Whistles more than 100 m apart: only one used for manoeuvring and warning signals.

ask.q: Is the one-short-blast signal an intention or an action?
ask.a: An action: 'I am altering my course to starboard'. It is sounded when the alteration is made, only between vessels in sight.

check.q: Three short blasts means:
options: I am altering course to port

topics.title: Sound signals in restricted visibility
topics.summary: In or near restricted visibility, signals are sounded at intervals of not more than 2 minutes. A power-driven vessel making way sounds one prolonged blast; underway but stopped, two prolonged. NUC, RAM, CBD, sailing, fishing and towing or pushing vessels sound one prolonged and two short.
points: Power-driven making way: one prolonged (2 min). Underway, not making way: two prolonged about 2 s apart (2 min).
NUC, RAM, CBD, sailing, fishing, towing or pushing: one prolonged + two short (2 min). Also fishing or RAM at anchor.
Manned towed vessel (last of the tow): one prolonged + three short, immediately after the towing vessel's signal if practicable.
At anchor: bell rung rapidly about 5 s every minute; at 100 m or more, bell forward then gong aft. May add short, prolonged, short as a warning.
Aground: anchor bell (and gong) plus three separate and distinct strokes on the bell before and after; may add a whistle signal.
Pilot vessel on duty: may add four short blasts. Under 12 m: any efficient sound signal every 2 min.

ask.q: You hear one prolonged and two short blasts. What could she be?
ask.a: NUC, RAM, CBD, a sailing vessel, a vessel engaged in fishing, or a vessel towing or pushing; also a fishing or RAM vessel at anchor.

ask.q: What is the anchor warning signal?
ask.a: One short, one prolonged and one short blast, to warn an approaching vessel of possible collision (Rule 35(g)).

check.q: A power-driven vessel underway but stopped in fog sounds:

topics.title: Signals to attract attention
topics.summary: Any vessel may make light or sound signals that cannot be mistaken for any authorised signal, or direct a searchlight beam towards a danger, provided she does not embarrass another vessel.
points: Lights used must not be mistaken for an aid to navigation.
High-intensity intermittent or revolving lights, such as strobe lights, should be avoided.

ask.q: Can you shine a searchlight at an approaching ship's bridge to attract attention?
ask.a: You may direct the beam in the direction of the danger, but not so as to embarrass (dazzle) the other vessel.

check.q: Under Rule 36, which should be avoided?
options: A searchlight directed at a danger

topics.title: Distress signals
topics.summary: A vessel in distress and requiring assistance uses or shows the signals in Annex IV.
points: See Annex IV for the full list.
Using a distress signal for any other purpose is prohibited.

ask.q: Is two all-round red lights a distress signal?
ask.a: No. That is NUC (Rule 27(a)); Rule 27(h) says NUC and RAM signals are not distress signals.

check.q: Distress signals are listed in:

topics.title: Exemptions
topics.summary: Ships whose keels were laid, or at a similar stage, before the 1972 Rules entered into force (15 July 1977) were given exemptions from some light and sound requirements, several of them permanent.
points: Examples: light ranges and colour specifications (time-limited), repositioning of lights after conversion to metric units, and some masthead light positions on ships under 150 m (permanent).
Rarely examined beyond knowing the rule exists and why.

ask.q: When did COLREGs 1972 enter into force?

check.q: Rule 38 concerns:

topics.title: Definitions (verification of compliance)
topics.summary: Part F, in force since 1 January 2016, defines the IMO Member State Audit Scheme, the IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code) and the audit standard.
points: Part F concerns flag States, not ships' crews.
Audit: a systematic, independent, documented process of obtaining evidence and evaluating it objectively.

ask.q: Who is audited under Part F?
ask.a: Contracting Governments (flag, coastal and port States), not individual ships.

check.q: Part F of the COLREGs deals with:
options: Verification of compliance by Contracting Parties

topics.title: Application (verification of compliance)
topics.summary: Contracting Parties use the III Code when carrying out their obligations under the Convention.
points: Links the COLREGs to the III Code for flag-State implementation.

ask.q: What is the III Code?
ask.a: The IMO Instruments Implementation Code: the standard States use to implement and enforce IMO conventions, and the basis for audits.

check.q: Under Rule 40, Contracting Parties use:

topics.title: Verification of compliance
topics.summary: Every Contracting Party is subject to periodic IMO audits under the audit standard, administered by the IMO Secretary-General.
points: Part of the mandatory IMO Member State Audit Scheme.

ask.q: Why might an examiner mention Part F?
ask.a: To check you know the COLREGs structure ends with Part F, and that it concerns State audits rather than shipboard practice.

check.q: Under Rule 41, audits are carried out by:
options: The flag State on its own ships

topics.title: Positioning and technical details of lights and shapes
topics.summary: Annex I sets light positions, spacing, colours and intensities, and the sizes of day shapes: ball, cone and cylinder at least 0.6 m in diameter, shapes at least 1.5 m apart.
points: Power-driven vessel of 20 m or more: forward masthead light at least 6 m above the hull (or the breadth if greater, up to 12 m); after masthead at least 4.5 m higher.
Masthead lights at least half the ship's length apart horizontally (not more than 100 m needed); the forward one not more than a quarter of the length from the stem.
Sidelights not higher than three-quarters of the forward masthead light height, and not in front of it.
Lights in a vertical line on vessels of 20 m or more: at least 2 m apart, the lowest at least 4 m above the hull (except a towing light).

Shapes: ball at least 0.6 m diameter; cone base 0.6 m and height equal to the diameter; cylinder 0.6 m diameter and twice as high; diamond is two cones base to base; at least 1.5 m between shapes. Smaller sizes allowed under 20 m.
Manoeuvring light: same fore-and-aft plane as the masthead lights, at least 2 m from them vertically where practicable.

ask.q: Give the minimum diameter of a ball shape and the spacing between shapes.
ask.a: 0.6 m diameter; at least 1.5 m apart.

check.q: The minimum vertical distance between day shapes (vessel of 20 m or more) is:

topics.title: Additional signals for fishing vessels fishing in close proximity
topics.summary: Trawlers of 20 m or more fishing near other fishing vessels show extra lights below their Rule 26 lights: two whites when shooting nets, white over red when hauling, two reds when nets are fast on an obstruction. Purse seiners may show two alternately flashing yellows.
points: Lights at least 0.9 m apart, lower than the Rule 26 lights, visible at least 1 nm (less than the Rule 26 lights).
Trawlers 20 m or more: shooting nets, two white; hauling nets, white over red; net fast on an obstruction, two red. Optional under 20 m.
Pair trawling: each vessel may direct a searchlight forward and towards the other.
Purse seiners hampered by gear: two yellow lights in a vertical line flashing alternately every second.

ask.q: A trawler shows green over white, and below them white over red. What is she doing?
ask.a: Trawling and hauling her nets (Annex II).

check.q: In Annex II, a trawler hauling her nets shows:

topics.title: Technical details of sound signal appliances
topics.summary: Whistle frequencies fall with length: 70 to 200 Hz for 200 m or more, 130 to 350 Hz for 75 to 200 m, 250 to 700 Hz under 75 m. Audibility ranges run from 2 nm (200 m or more) down to 0.5 nm (under 20 m).
points: Audibility: 200 m or more, 2 nm; 75 to 200 m, 1.5 nm; 20 to 75 m, 1 nm; under 20 m, 0.5 nm.
Bell mouth diameter: at least 300 mm for vessels of 20 m or more; 200 mm for 12 to 20 m.
A deeper whistle note suggests a larger ship.

ask.q: Why do larger ships have lower-pitched whistles?
ask.a: Lower frequencies carry further, and the pitch gives a clue to the vessel's size (Annex III).

check.q: Whistle audibility range for a vessel of 200 m or more:

topics.title: Distress signals
topics.summary: Annex IV lists the signals that indicate distress and need of assistance, from red flares and orange smoke to MAYDAY, DSC alerts, EPIRBs and SARTs. Using them for anything else is prohibited.
points: Gun or explosive signal at about one-minute intervals; continuous sounding of any fog-signal apparatus.
Rockets or shells throwing red stars; red parachute flare or red hand flare; orange smoke.
SOS (... --- ...) by any signalling method; MAYDAY by radiotelephony.
Flags N over C; a square flag with a ball (or anything like one) above or below it; flames on the vessel.
Slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering arms outstretched to each side.
DSC distress alert (VHF ch 70, MF/HF); ship-to-shore alert by Inmarsat or another mobile satellite service; EPIRB signals; approved radio signals including SARTs.
Also noted: orange canvas with a black square and circle for air identification, and a dye marker.

ask.q: Name six distress signals.
ask.a: Any six from Annex IV, e.g. red parachute flare, orange smoke, SOS, MAYDAY, NC flags, continuous fog signal, DSC alert, EPIRB, flames, arm signal.

ask.q: What do you do after a false distress alert from your ship?
ask.a: Cancel it at once: reset the equipment and broadcast a voice cancellation on the associated distress channel, inform the RCC, and log it.

check.q: Which is NOT an Annex IV distress signal?
options: Continuous sounding of a fog signal
check.why: Two all-round reds is NUC (Rule 27(a)); Rule 27(h) says it is not a distress signal.

topics.title: The IALA system and the two regions
topics.summary: The IALA Maritime Buoyage System uses six types of mark: lateral, cardinal, isolated danger, safe water, special and emergency wreck. The world is split into Region A and Region B, which differ only in the colours of lateral marks.
points: Region A: red to port, green to starboard (Europe, Africa including Nigeria, most of Asia, Australia).
Region B: green to port, red to starboard ('red right returning'): the Americas, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines.
Shapes, topmarks and all non-lateral marks are the same in both regions.
Identify a mark in this order: colour, shape, topmark, then light colour and rhythm.
Check the region on the chart, in the List of Lights, Sailing Directions or NP 735 (IALA buoyage).

ask.q: What differs between Region A and Region B?
ask.a: Only the colour of lateral marks and their lights. Everything else is identical.

ask.q: Which region are Nigerian waters in?
ask.a: Region A.

check.q: In IALA Region B a port-hand lateral mark is:
check.why: Region B reverses lateral colours; shapes stay the same, so port is a green can.

topics.title: Lateral marks and direction of buoyage
topics.summary: Lateral marks show the port and starboard sides of a channel, read in the conventional direction of buoyage. Port marks are cans, starboard marks are cones (or pillars and spars with those topmarks).
points: Direction of buoyage: from seaward when approaching a harbour, river or estuary; elsewhere set by the authorities, generally clockwise round landmasses. Charts show it with an arrow where it is not obvious.
Port (Region A): red can, red can topmark, red light of any rhythm except Fl(2+1).
Starboard (Region A): green cone, cone point-up topmark, green light of any rhythm except Fl(2+1).
Marks may be numbered or lettered in the direction of buoyage; the chart shows the numbering used locally.
Outbound, leave port marks to starboard.

ask.q: Outbound from a Region A port, which side do you leave a green cone?
ask.a: To port: lateral marks are read in the direction of buoyage, which is inbound.

ask.q: You see a green flashing light ahead at night. What could it be?
ask.a: A starboard lateral in Region A, a port lateral in Region B, or a Region A preferred-channel-to-port mark if it is Fl(2+1) G. Check the chart.

check.q: The conventional direction of buoyage when approaching a harbour is:
options: From the harbour towards the sea
check.why: Approaching a harbour, river or estuary, the direction of buoyage is from seaward.

topics.title: Preferred channel marks
topics.summary: At a channel junction, a modified lateral mark shows the preferred channel. It carries one broad horizontal band of the other colour and shows a Fl(2+1) light.
points: Preferred channel to starboard (Region A): red can with one broad green band, Fl(2+1) R. Leave it to port to stay in the preferred channel.
Preferred channel to port (Region A): green cone with one broad red band, Fl(2+1) G. Leave it to starboard.
In Region B the colours reverse.
Fl(2+1) is reserved for preferred channel marks.

ask.q: A red can with a green band: which side do you leave it to stay in the main channel?
ask.a: Leave it to port (Region A). It is a modified port-hand mark; the preferred channel is to starboard.

check.q: The light rhythm reserved for preferred channel marks is:

topics.title: Cardinal marks
topics.summary: Cardinal marks show where the safest water is, relative to a danger, by compass quadrant. The topmark cones point to the black parts of the mark. Lights are white, quick or very quick, with flashes matching a clock face.
points: North: cones both up, black over yellow; VQ or Q continuous.
East: cones base to base, black-yellow-black; VQ(3) 5 s or Q(3) 10 s.
South: cones both down, yellow over black; VQ(6)+LFl 10 s or Q(6)+LFl 15 s.
West: cones point to point, yellow-black-yellow; VQ(9) 10 s or Q(9) 15 s.
Uses: mark the deepest water, the safe side of a danger, a bend, junction or fork, or the end of a shoal.
Pass on the named side: north of a north cardinal.

ask.q: Why does the south cardinal add a long flash?
ask.a: To make six flashes easy to tell from three or nine.

ask.q: Give two memory aids for cardinal topmarks.
ask.a: Cones point to the black bands; West looks like a 'W' or a wineglass waist, East like an egg.

check.q: A mark with two black cones point to point and yellow-black-yellow bands is:
check.why: West cardinal: cones point to point (wineglass), yellow-black-yellow.

topics.title: Isolated danger mark
topics.summary: An isolated danger mark sits on, or moored above, a danger of limited extent with navigable water all round. It is black with red bands, two black spheres, and a white Fl(2) light.
points: Colour: black with one or more broad horizontal red bands.
Topmark: two black spheres. Light: Fl(2) white: two spheres, two flashes.
Give it a good berth; check the charted extent of the danger.

ask.q: Which side do you pass an isolated danger mark?
ask.a: Either side, with a good berth, having checked the chart for the extent of the danger.

check.q: The light of an isolated danger mark is:

topics.title: Safe water mark
topics.summary: A safe water mark shows navigable water all round: a fairway, mid-channel or landfall. It is red and white vertically striped with a single red sphere, and a white isophase, occulting, long-flash or Morse A light.
points: Colour: red and white vertical stripes. Shape: spherical, pillar or spar. Topmark: one red sphere.
Light: white Iso, Oc, LFl 10 s or Mo(A).

ask.q: Which marks use vertical stripes?
ask.a: Safe water marks (red and white) and emergency wreck marks (blue and yellow).

check.q: A safe water mark's topmark is:

topics.title: Special marks
topics.summary: Special marks are yellow with a yellow X topmark and a yellow light. They mark a special area or feature, not primarily for navigation.
points: Examples: ODAS buoys, spoil grounds, military exercise areas, cables or pipelines, recreation zones, TSS where lateral marks could confuse.
Shape is optional but should not conflict with nearby lateral marks.
Light: yellow, any rhythm not used for white-light marks.

ask.q: What is an ODAS buoy?
ask.a: An Ocean Data Acquisition System buoy, collecting weather or oceanographic data, marked as a special mark.

check.q: A special mark's light is:

topics.title: Emergency wreck marking buoy
topics.summary: An emergency wreck marking buoy marks a newly discovered wreck until it is surveyed, promulgated and permanently marked. It has blue and yellow vertical stripes and an alternating blue and yellow light.
points: Stripes: 4 to 8 blue and yellow, vertical. Topmark (optional): upright yellow cross.
Light: alternating blue and yellow, 1 s each with 0.5 s dark between.
May carry a racon coded Morse D and/or an AIS AtoN.
Blue is used nowhere else in the buoyage system.

ask.q: What does a racon coded D look like on radar?
ask.a: Dash dot dot (-..) painted radially outward beyond the buoy's echo.

check.q: The racon code of an emergency wreck marking buoy is:

topics.title: Light characters
topics.summary: A light's character is its colour, rhythm and period. Learn the abbreviations and how to time a light with a stopwatch or by counting.
points: F fixed; Fl flashing (light shorter than dark); LFl long flash (at least 2 s); Q quick (50 to 79 per minute, usually 60); VQ very quick (80 to 159, usually 100 or 120).
Iso isophase (equal light and dark); Oc occulting (light longer than dark); Mo(A) Morse code letter; Al alternating colours.
Groups: Fl(2) two flashes; Fl(2+1) composite group; Q(6)+LFl six quick then a long flash.
Period: time from the start of one sequence to the start of the next. Time several cycles to confirm.
Cross-check against the chart and the List of Lights, and by radar or AIS AtoN.

ask.q: Difference between occulting and isophase?
ask.a: Occulting: light longer than dark. Isophase: equal durations of light and dark.

ask.q: How do you identify a light reliably at night?
ask.a: Note colour, count and time the rhythm over several periods with a stopwatch, then compare with the chart and List of Lights; confirm with radar range and bearing.

check.q: Quick flashing (Q) is:

topics.title: Using buoyage safely
topics.summary: Buoys can drag, sink, be unlit or be moved. Use them to confirm position, never as the only fix, and check the chart, Notices to Mariners and navigational warnings.
points: Floating marks may be off station; fix the ship's position by fixed objects or other means.
Lights can be extinguished; topmarks can be missing.
AIS AtoN may be real (on the buoy), synthetic (transmitted from shore for a real buoy) or virtual (no physical mark).
A new danger may be marked by duplicated marks and a racon coded D until it is promulgated.

ask.q: What is a virtual AIS AtoN?
ask.a: An AIS aid to navigation transmitted for a position where no physical mark exists, shown on ECDIS or radar as a symbol.

check.q: Floating marks should be used:
options: As the primary means of fixing position
To confirm position, alongside other methods
check.why: Buoys may be off station; do not rely on them alone.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Port-hand lateral mark (Region A)
pictures.sum: Leave it to port when proceeding in the direction of buoyage.

follow.q: What sets the direction of buoyage?
follow.a: Approach from seaward; elsewhere the authority sets it, generally clockwise round landmasses; the chart shows an arrow where needed.

follow.q: Which region are Nigerian waters, and who uses Region B?
follow.a: Region A. Region B: the Americas, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines.

follow.q: Topmark missing and light out: how do you still identify it?
follow.a: Shape, colour, charted position, name or number, radar and AIS AtoN.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Starboard-hand lateral mark (Region A)
pictures.sum: Leave it to starboard when proceeding in the direction of buoyage.

follow.q: Outbound, which side do you leave it?
follow.a: To port.

follow.q: A green flashing light ahead at night: what could it be?
follow.a: Starboard lateral (Region A), port lateral (Region B), or preferred channel to port if Fl(2+1) G. A ship's sidelight is fixed, not flashing.

pictures.scen: Inbound to a port in the United States.
pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Port-hand lateral mark (Region B)
pictures.sum: Region B reverses the lateral colours: green to port, red to starboard. Shapes stay the same.

follow.a: In Region B, keep red marks to starboard when returning from sea.
Only lateral colours and their light colours.

follow.q: Where do you confirm the region?
follow.a: Chart, List of Lights, Sailing Directions, NP 735.

pictures.scen: Inbound to a port in the United States.
pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Starboard-hand lateral mark (Region B)
pictures.sum: Red right returning: leave it to starboard inbound.

follow.a: Leave it to starboard.

follow.q: The same mark in Region A?
follow.a: A green cone.

pictures.scen: IALA Region A, approaching a channel junction.
pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Preferred channel to starboard (Region A)
pictures.sum: A modified port-hand mark. Leave it to port to follow the preferred channel, which lies to starboard.
facts: Red with one broad green band

follow.q: To stay in the main channel, which side do you leave it?
follow.a: To port.
Green can with a red band, Fl(2+1) G.
At channel junctions and bifurcations.

pictures.scen: IALA Region A, approaching a channel junction.
pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Preferred channel to port (Region A)
pictures.sum: A modified starboard-hand mark. Leave it to starboard to follow the preferred channel, which lies to port.
facts: Green with one broad red band

follow.q: Which side do you leave it to stay in the main channel?
follow.a: To starboard: the preferred channel is to port.

follow.q: Which rhythm is reserved for these marks?

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: North cardinal mark
pictures.sum: The safe water lies to the north. Pass to the north of it.
facts: Two black cones, both point up

follow.q: Give all four cardinal light rhythms.
follow.a: N: VQ or Q. E: VQ(3) 5 s or Q(3) 10 s. S: VQ(6)+LFl 10 s or Q(6)+LFl 15 s. W: VQ(9) 10 s or Q(9) 15 s.

follow.q: What are cardinal marks used for?
follow.a: To show the deepest water, the safe side of a danger, a bend, junction or fork, or the end of a shoal.

follow.q: Heading 270, which side of you will it be as you pass safely?
follow.a: On your port side: you pass to the north of it.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: East cardinal mark
pictures.sum: The safe water lies to the east. Pass to the east of it.
facts: Two black cones, base to base
VQ(3) W 5 s or Q(3) W 10 s

follow.q: Memory aid for topmarks and bands?
follow.a: The cones point to the black bands.
East is 3 o'clock: three flashes.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: South cardinal mark
pictures.sum: The safe water lies to the south. Pass to the south of it.
facts: Two black cones, both point down
VQ(6)+LFl W 10 s or Q(6)+LFl W 15 s

follow.a: So six cannot be confused with three or nine.

follow.q: Heading 090, which side of you as you pass safely?
follow.a: On your port side: you pass to the south of it.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: West cardinal mark
pictures.sum: The safe water lies to the west. Pass to the west of it.
facts: Two black cones, point to point
VQ(9) W 10 s or Q(9) W 15 s

follow.q: Flashes per minute for Q and VQ?
follow.a: Q 50 to 79 (usually 60); VQ 80 to 159 (usually 100 or 120).
Cones point to point like a wineglass or a waist: West.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Isolated danger mark
pictures.sum: Marks a danger of limited extent with navigable water all round. Give it a good berth.
facts: Black with one or more broad red bands

follow.a: Two spheres, two flashes.
Either side, with a good berth; check the charted extent.

follow.q: How is a newly discovered danger marked?
follow.a: With normal marks (possibly duplicated), a racon coded D, and NAVTEX and NAVAREA warnings; or an emergency wreck marking buoy.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Safe water mark
pictures.sum: Navigable water all round: a fairway, mid-channel or landfall mark.
facts: White: Iso, Oc, LFl 10 s or Mo(A)

follow.a: Safe water (red and white) and emergency wreck marks (blue and yellow).
White Iso, Oc, LFl 10 s or Mo(A).

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Special mark
pictures.sum: Marks a special area or feature: ODAS buoy, spoil ground, cable or pipeline, exercise or recreation area.
facts: Yellow, any rhythm not used by white-light marks

follow.q: Give examples of what a special mark may show.
follow.a: ODAS buoy, spoil ground, exercise area, cable or pipeline, recreation zone, TSS where lateral marks could confuse.

follow.q: Why might it be can- or cone-shaped?
follow.a: The shape follows the lateral side when it marks a channel edge.

pictures.q: Identify this mark. Where is the safe water, and how do you pass it?
pictures.title: Emergency wreck marking buoy
pictures.sum: Marks a new wreck until it is surveyed, promulgated and permanently marked. Keep well clear.
facts: Blue and yellow vertical stripes (4 to 8)
Alternating Bu and Y, 1 s each with 0.5 s dark
Racon Morse D and/or AIS AtoN

follow.a: Once the wreck is surveyed, promulgated and permanently marked.
As close as practicable to the wreck, or in a pattern round it.

follow.q: What does a racon coded D look like on radar?
follow.a: Dash dot dot painted radially beyond the echo.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: North cardinal mark
pictures.sum: Very quick white, never interrupted. Quick white, uninterrupted, is also North.
facts: VQ 80 to 159 per min, Q 50 to 79

follow.q: How do you tell VQ from Q by eye?
follow.a: Count for 10 s: VQ gives about 17 to 20 flashes, Q about 8 to 10.
To the north.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: East cardinal mark
pictures.sum: Three quick flashes every 10 s. The very quick version is VQ(3) every 5 s.

follow.a: VQ(3) every 5 s.
To the east.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: South cardinal mark
pictures.sum: Six very quick flashes and a long flash every 10 s. The quick version is Q(6)+LFl every 15 s.
facts: At least 2 s, so six is not mistaken for three or nine

follow.a: Q(6)+LFl every 15 s.

follow.q: Minimum length of a long flash?
follow.a: 2 seconds.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: West cardinal mark
pictures.sum: Nine quick flashes every 15 s. The very quick version is VQ(9) every 10 s.

follow.a: VQ(9) every 10 s.

follow.q: You counted eight flashes. Now what?
follow.a: Watch another cycle, check the chart and List of Lights, confirm with radar and AIS AtoN.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: Isolated danger mark
pictures.sum: Group of two white flashes: two flashes, two black spheres.
facts: Either side, with a good berth
Chart and List of Lights for the period

follow.a: Two black spheres.

follow.q: Could Fl(2) W be something else?
follow.a: Yes, a lighthouse or beacon with that character; check the chart and List of Lights.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: Safe water mark
pictures.sum: One long white flash every 10 s.

follow.q: Other permitted characters for this mark?
follow.a: Iso, Oc, Mo(A).

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: Safe water mark
pictures.sum: Morse A, short then long.

follow.a: Dot dash: short then long.
Fairway, landfall or mid-channel.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: Preferred channel to starboard (Region A)
pictures.sum: Composite group flashing red: a modified port-hand mark. Leave it to port to stay in the preferred channel.
facts: Fl(2+1) is used only on preferred-channel marks
Fl(2+1) R marks preferred channel to port

follow.q: Which side to stay in the main channel?
follow.a: Leave it to port.
Preferred channel to port: a modified starboard-hand mark.

pictures.q: Count the light. What could it be?
pictures.title: Starboard lateral (Region A) or port lateral (Region B)
pictures.sum: Green lateral light. The region and its position relative to the channel decide which side you leave it.
facts: Chart, List of Lights, radar, AIS AtoN

follow.q: Why can the light alone not settle it?
follow.a: It depends on the region and on its position relative to the channel.
Chart, List of Lights, radar, AIS AtoN.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: Port-hand lateral mark (Region A)
pictures.sum: Quick red. Lateral lights may use any rhythm except Fl(2+1); Q often marks a bend or hazard.

follow.a: Any rhythm except Fl(2+1).

follow.q: Why use Q on a lateral mark?
follow.a: For emphasis at a bend or hazard.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: Special mark
pictures.sum: Yellow light, any rhythm not used by cardinal, isolated danger or safe water marks.

follow.q: Rhythms a special mark cannot use?
follow.a: Those of cardinal, isolated danger and safe water marks.
Towing light, a purse seiner's alternating yellows, an air-cushion vessel's flashing yellow.

pictures.q: Count the light. What mark is it?
pictures.title: Emergency wreck marking buoy
pictures.char: Al Bu Y (1 s + 0.5 s dark each)
pictures.sum: Alternating blue and yellow flashes. Blue is used nowhere else in the buoyage system.
facts: Keep well clear; check NAVTEX and NAVAREA warnings

follow.a: Blue is used nowhere else in the buoyage system.
Keep well clear, check NAVTEX and NAVAREA warnings, report it if not promulgated.

pictures.scen: Right ahead, bearing steady, range closing.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Power-driven vessel, 50 m or more, head-on
pictures.sum: Masthead lights in line with both sidelights: you are meeting on reciprocal courses.
facts: Two masthead lights, aft one higher; both sidelights
Both alter to starboard and pass port to port; one short blast

follow.a: Both alter to starboard and pass port to port; one short blast (Rule 34(a)).
Assume head-on (Rule 14(c)).
Masthead 6 nm, sidelights 3 nm (Rule 22).
225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft each beam.

pictures.scen: On your port bow, bearing steady, range closing.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Power-driven vessel, 50 m or more, starboard side
pictures.sum: Masthead lights open with the lower forward light to your right and her green showing: she is crossing from your port side.
facts: Keep course and speed; act under 17(a)(ii) or 17(b) if she does not; do not alter to port for her

follow.a: Keep course and speed (17(a)(i)); you may act once she clearly is not (17(a)(ii)); you must act when she alone cannot avoid collision (17(b)).
Altering to port for a vessel on your own port side (17(c)).
At least five short and rapid blasts (Rule 34(d)).

follow.q: How do you confirm risk of collision?
follow.a: Steady compass bearing, ARPA CPA and TCPA (Rule 7).

pictures.scen: On your starboard bow, bearing steady, range closing.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Power-driven vessel, 50 m or more, port side
pictures.sum: Forward (lower) masthead light to your left and her red showing, on your starboard side.
facts: Early, substantial alteration to starboard to pass astern of her; or slow, stop or go astern

follow.a: Early and substantial, normally to starboard to pass astern of her; do not cross ahead (Rules 15, 16).

follow.q: If you cannot alter to starboard?
follow.a: Reduce speed, stop or go astern (Rule 8(e)).

follow.q: How do you check it worked?
follow.a: Bearing opening and CPA increasing, until finally past and clear (Rule 8(d)).

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Power-driven vessel under 50 m, head-on
pictures.sum: One masthead light and both sidelights. A second masthead light is optional under 50 m.
facts: Alter to starboard, one short blast
Masthead 5 nm (3 nm under 20 m), sidelights 2 nm

follow.q: Masthead light range for 20 to 50 m?
follow.a: 5 nm (3 nm under 20 m).
If so she must show two masthead lights; suspect a failed light.

pictures.scen: Fine on your bow. You are the faster ship.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel ahead, sternlight only
pictures.sum: Only her white sternlight shows, so you are more than 22.5° abaft her beam: you are overtaking.
facts: Keep out of the way until finally past and clear

follow.a: Coming up from more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam.
Keep out of the way until finally past and clear (Rule 13).

follow.q: What else shows a single white light?
follow.a: A vessel under 50 m at anchor, a small power-driven or sailing vessel, a vessel under oars with a torch.
Two prolonged + one short (your starboard side); two prolonged + two short (your port side); agreement prolonged, short, prolonged, short.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Sailing vessel underway, head-on
pictures.sum: All-round red over green at the masthead (optional) with sidelights. No masthead light.
facts: A power-driven vessel keeps out of her way, subject to Rules 9, 10 and 13
None under sail; cone apex down if also motoring

follow.q: Your duty as a power-driven vessel?
follow.a: Keep out of her way (Rule 18), subject to Rules 9, 10 and 13.

follow.q: She starts her engine. What changes?
follow.a: She becomes a power-driven vessel; by day she shows a cone apex down.

follow.q: Can she show this with a tricolour lantern?
follow.a: No.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Sailing vessel under 20 m, tricolour lantern
pictures.sum: A single green high on the mast from a combined lantern: you see her starboard side.
facts: Keep out of her way as a power-driven vessel
Tricolour and red-over-green must not be shown together

follow.a: Sailing vessels show no masthead light; the tricolour's white sector faces astern.

follow.q: Two sailing vessels meeting: which rule?
follow.a: Rule 12.
Small radar echo, dim light high on the mast, easily lost against shore lights.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Trawling, making way, starboard side
pictures.sum: Green over white all-round, a masthead light abaft and higher, and her green sidelight.
facts: Keep clear (Rule 18); she must not impede in a narrow channel or TSS lane

follow.a: Two cones, apexes together.
Two white: shooting nets; white over red: hauling nets; two red: nets fast on an obstruction.

follow.q: Does green over white mean she is making way?
follow.a: No. Sidelights and sternlight show that.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Fishing other than trawling, gear out over 150 m
pictures.sum: Red over white all-round and her red sidelight, plus a lower all-round white showing the direction of outlying gear.
facts: Keep clear and pass away from the gear light
Two cones apexes together; cone apex up towards the gear

follow.a: Away from the gear light.
A cone apex upwards towards the gear.
Two yellow lights flashing alternately every second (Annex II).
She must not impede vessels following the lane (Rule 10(i)).

pictures.scen: On your port bow, bearing steady.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Not under command, making way
pictures.sum: Two all-round reds with a sidelight and no masthead lights: NUC, making way, starboard side.

follow.a: Only the two all-round reds.
Two balls.
One prolonged, two short (Rule 35(c)).
She is still an anchored vessel and shows anchor signals.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Restricted in ability to manoeuvre, making way
pictures.sum: Red-white-red all-round with masthead lights and her red sidelight: port side.

follow.a: Ball, diamond, ball.
Cable or pipeline work, dredging, surveying, transfer under way, aircraft operations, mine clearance, restrictive towing.

follow.q: Is an STS transfer under way RAM?
follow.a: Yes, Rule 3(g)(iii).
Red-white-red plus anchor lights.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Dredging, obstruction on one side
pictures.sum: Red-white-red with two reds on the obstructed side (your left) and two greens on the side you may pass (your right). Not making way.
facts: On the side of the two greens
Ball-diamond-ball; two balls obstructed side; two diamonds clear side

follow.a: On the side of the greens.
Ball-diamond-ball; two balls on the obstructed side; two diamonds on the side to pass.

follow.q: At anchor, does she add anchor lights?
follow.a: No. These replace them (27(d)(iii)).

pictures.scen: On your port bow, in a buoyed channel.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Constrained by her draught
pictures.sum: Power-driven vessel lights plus three all-round reds: starboard side.
facts: Avoid impeding her safe passage if circumstances admit

follow.a: Cylinder.
Avoid impeding her if circumstances admit (Rule 18(d)).

follow.q: Is she then the stand-on vessel?
follow.a: Not automatically. Once risk of collision develops, the steering rules apply (Rule 8(f)).

follow.q: When might a laden LNG carrier show it?
follow.a: In a restricted channel where her draught limits deviation, on the Master's decision.

pictures.scen: Broad on your starboard bow, bearing drawing aft.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel at anchor, 50 m or more
pictures.sum: Two all-round whites, the forward one higher. At 100 m or more she must also light her decks.
facts: Masthead lights: forward light lower, with sidelights

follow.a: Anchor lights: forward light higher, no sidelights, aspect never changes.

follow.q: Extra requirement at 100 m or more?
follow.a: Deck working lights (Rule 30(c)).
One ball forward.

follow.q: Fog signal at 100 m or more?
follow.a: Bell forward and gong aft every minute; may add short, prolonged, short (Rule 35(g)).

pictures.scen: Near a charted shoal on your port bow.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel aground
pictures.sum: Anchor lights plus two all-round reds in a vertical line.
facts: Anchor bell signal with three distinct strokes before and after

follow.a: Three balls in a vertical line.
Anchor signal with three separate and distinct bell strokes before and after (Rule 35(h)).

follow.q: Your own ship goes aground on your watch. Actions?
follow.a: Stop engines, alarm, Master, signals, soundings round the ship, hull and tank checks, position, tide, report, save VDR data.

pictures.scen: Right ahead, near the pilot station.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Pilot vessel on duty, underway, head-on
pictures.sum: White over red all-round at the masthead with both sidelights.
facts: White over red plus anchor light

follow.a: White over red plus anchor light(s).
Four short blasts (Rule 35(k)).
Ladder rigged to SOLAS V/23, lee, speed, officer with radio, lighting, lifebuoy with light.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Towing, length of tow over 200 m
pictures.sum: Three masthead lights in a vertical line and a green sidelight; the separate green astern is the tow’s sidelight.

follow.a: Diamond on tug and tow.
Tug: one prolonged + two short. Manned tow: one prolonged + three short.
From the tug's stern to the after end of the tow.
Pass between tug and tow.

pictures.scen: Ahead of you. You are the faster ship.
pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Tug and tow, seen from astern
pictures.sum: The nearer white is the tow’s sternlight. The yellow towing light above a white sternlight ahead of it is the tug.
facts: Yellow, same 135° arc as a sternlight
Overtake well clear of the whole tow

follow.a: 135 degrees, the same as a sternlight.

follow.q: Overtaking a tow: what do you allow for?
follow.a: Its total length, yaw, the towline catenary, and CPA from both tug and tow.

follow.q: A pushing tug seen from astern?
follow.a: Sternlight only, no towing light.
