pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Towing (tow 200 m or less), or pushing ahead
pictures.sum: Two masthead lights in a vertical line with both sidelights. From ahead you cannot tell towing from pushing.
facts: Tow’s lights, radar, AIS; from astern only a towing vessel shows the yellow towing light

follow.a: Look for the tow's lights, radar and AIS; from astern only a towing vessel shows the yellow towing light.
Lit as one power-driven vessel.
She adds an after masthead light.

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Air-cushion vessel, non-displacement mode
pictures.sum: Power-driven vessel lights plus an all-round flashing yellow.
facts: Treat as a power-driven vessel: head-on, alter to starboard

follow.a: 120 or more flashes per minute (Rule 21(f)).
A high-intensity all-round flashing red when taking off, landing or flying near the surface (Rule 23(c)).

pictures.q: What is she, which aspect are you seeing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel engaged in mine clearance
pictures.sum: Power-driven vessel lights plus three all-round greens at the foremast head and the ends of the fore yard.
facts: Three balls in the same positions

follow.a: Three balls in the same places.
Restricted in ability to manoeuvre (Rule 3(g)(v)).

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel at anchor
pictures.sum: One ball in the forepart, where it can best be seen.
facts: Anchor lights; deck lights at 100 m or more
Under 7 m, clear of channels, fairways and anchorages

follow.q: Night equivalent, and the extra at 100 m or more?
follow.a: Forward anchor light higher than aft; deck lights.
Bell rung rapidly for about 5 s every minute; at 100 m or more a gong aft as well; may add short, prolonged, short (Rule 35(g)).
A vessel under 7 m at anchor clear of channels, fairways and anchorages (Rule 30(e)).

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Not under command
pictures.sum: Two balls in a vertical line, where they can best be seen.
facts: Two all-round reds; sidelights and sternlight when making way

follow.a: Main engine or steering failure; any exceptional circumstance that stops her manoeuvring as the Rules require.

follow.q: Which vessels must keep out of her way?
follow.a: Power-driven, sailing and fishing vessels (Rule 18).
The anchor ball.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Restricted in ability to manoeuvre
pictures.sum: Ball, diamond, ball in a vertical line, where they can best be seen.
facts: Cable or pipeline work, surveying, transfer under way, launching aircraft

follow.q: Name four RAM activities from Rule 3(g).
follow.a: Buoy, cable or pipeline work; dredging, surveying or underwater work; replenishment or transfer under way; aircraft operations; mine clearance; restrictive towing.

follow.q: Is a ship with a steering failure RAM?
follow.a: No, NUC. RAM comes from the nature of her work.

follow.q: What does she add at anchor?
follow.a: The anchor ball (Rule 27(b)(iv)).

pictures.scen: On your port bow, in a buoyed channel.
pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Constrained by her draught
pictures.sum: A cylinder, where it can best be seen.
facts: Three all-round reds with power-driven vessel lights
Avoid impeding her safe passage if circumstances admit

follow.a: The Master, judging draught against available depth and width.

follow.q: Must a fishing vessel avoid impeding her?
follow.a: Yes: every vessel except NUC and RAM, if circumstances admit (Rule 18(d)(i)).

follow.q: What does Rule 18(d)(ii) require of her?
follow.a: To navigate with particular caution.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel aground
pictures.sum: Three balls in a vertical line, where they can best be seen.
facts: Two balls means not under command
Anchor lights plus two all-round reds

follow.q: How do you tell this from mine clearance?
follow.a: Mine clearance balls sit at the masthead and the yard ends, not in a vertical line.
Anchor bell with three separate and distinct strokes before and after (Rule 35(h)).

follow.q: What does it tell you about your own navigation?
follow.a: There is shoal water near her; check your position and UKC.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel engaged in fishing (here trawling)
pictures.sum: Two cones with their apexes together in a vertical line. Trawlers and other fishing vessels show the same shape.
facts: Same two cones; the old basket option was deleted in 1995
Fishing shapes only, no anchor ball

follow.a: A basket.

follow.q: Is a vessel trolling lines engaged in fishing?
follow.a: No: the gear must restrict manoeuvrability (Rule 3(d)).
The same shape, no anchor ball (Rule 26(a)).

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Fishing other than trawling, gear out over 150 m
pictures.sum: Two cones apexes together, plus a cone apex upwards on the side the gear extends: her port side, your right.
facts: On your left, away from the gear
All-round white light towards the gear

follow.a: On your left, her starboard side, away from the gear.

follow.q: Night equivalent of the gear cone?
follow.a: An all-round white light towards the gear.

follow.q: Does a trawler show this cone?
follow.a: No, only a vessel fishing other than trawling.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Towing, length of tow over 200 m
pictures.sum: A diamond on the towing vessel and a diamond on the tow.
facts: From the tug’s stern to the after end of the tow

follow.a: No shape required.

follow.q: Tow partly submerged and hard to see?

Well clear of both, never between them.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Sailing vessel also using her engine

facts: Apply the power-driven vessel rules: meeting, crossing, overtaking

follow.q: Crossing from your port side, bearing steady: who gives way?

Power-driven vessel lights, including a masthead light.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Dredging, obstruction on one side
pictures.sum: Ball-diamond-ball, with two balls on the obstructed side (your left) and two diamonds on the side you may pass (your right).
facts: On the side of the two diamonds
These shapes replace the anchor ball

follow.a: The side of the two diamonds.

follow.q: At anchor, does she add the anchor ball?
follow.a: No; these shapes replace it (27(d)(iii)).
Red-white-red; two reds on the obstructed side; two greens on the clear side.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Restricted in ability to manoeuvre, at anchor
pictures.sum: Ball-diamond-ball plus the anchor ball forward.
facts: Survey or cable work while at anchor
A dredger with an obstruction shows no anchor ball

follow.q: Why does she add the anchor ball when a dredger does not?
follow.a: Rule 27(b) adds the Rule 30 signals; 27(d) replaces them.
Red-white-red plus anchor lights.

pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Vessel engaged in mine clearance
pictures.sum: Three balls: one near the foremast head and one at each end of the fore yard.
facts: Three balls in a vertical line means aground

follow.a: Not within 1000 m.

follow.q: How does it differ from aground?
follow.a: The arrangement: aground is a vertical line.
Three all-round greens in the same places.

pictures.scen: Close inshore, fine on your starboard bow.
pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Small vessel engaged in diving operations
pictures.sum: A rigid replica of International Code flag A, at least 1 m high, visible all round.

follow.a: I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed.
Red-white-red all-round lights.
Slow down, give a wide berth, look out for divers' bubbles and surface markers.

pictures.scen: On your port bow, in a channel.
pictures.q: What is she showing, and what do you do?
pictures.title: Towing, unable to deviate from her course
pictures.sum: The tug shows ball-diamond-ball as well as the towing diamond; the tow shows a diamond.

follow.a: Restricted in her ability to manoeuvre.
Towing lights plus red-white-red.
A heavy tow in a narrow channel, or a rig tow.

verbal.q: In fog you detect a target by radar alone, forward of the beam, closing. What does Rule 19 require?
verbal.a: No stand-on or give-way vessel. Decide whether a close-quarters situation or risk exists; if so act in ample time. Avoid altering to port for a vessel forward of the beam (unless she is being overtaken) and avoid altering towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam. Safe speed, engines ready, fog signals, Master called.

follow.a: Section II, including stand-on and give-way, applies only to vessels in sight (Rule 11).

follow.q: You then hear her fog signal forward of the beam. What now?
follow.a: Reduce to bare steerage way, take all way off if necessary, navigate with extreme caution (Rule 19(e)).

verbal.q: What factors decide a safe speed?
verbal.a: Visibility; traffic density; stopping distance and turning ability; background light at night; wind, sea, current and hazards; draught against depth. With radar: its limits, range scale, clutter and interference, small targets it may miss, number and movement of targets, the better estimate of visibility (Rule 6).

follow.q: What is your safe speed entering a busy port approach in fog?
follow.a: No single figure: a speed that lets you stop or manoeuvre in time given visibility, traffic and radar performance, engines on standby.

follow.q: Can a safe speed ever be full speed?
follow.a: Yes, in clear visibility, open water and light traffic, if action and stopping in time remain possible.

verbal.q: How do you establish risk of collision?
verbal.a: All available means. A steady compass bearing with decreasing range; risk may exist even with a changing bearing for a large vessel, a tow or at close range. Proper radar use with plotting or ARPA; no assumptions on scanty information; if in doubt, risk exists (Rule 7).

follow.q: Why a compass bearing rather than a relative one?
follow.a: Relative bearings change with your own heading and yaw.

follow.q: ARPA shows CPA 1.2 nm. Is there risk?
follow.a: Depends on the circumstances and standing orders; ARPA data has errors and lags. Monitor and be ready to act.

verbal.q: Describe the action required by Rule 8.
verbal.a: Positive, in ample time, good seamanship; large enough to be readily apparent; no series of small alterations; course alteration alone may be best with sea room; pass at a safe distance; check until finally past and clear; slow, stop or reverse if necessary.

follow.q: What does 'not impede' in Rule 8(f) require once risk exists?
follow.a: The vessel required not to impede is still bound by that duty and must also follow the steering rules; the other vessel must follow the steering rules too.

follow.q: What size of alteration is 'readily apparent'?
follow.a: Typically 30 degrees or more, or a substantial speed change.

verbal.q: How do you navigate in a traffic separation scheme?
verbal.a: Use the lane in the direction of flow; keep clear of the separation line or zone; join or leave at the ends or at a small angle; cross at right angles on heading; do not use inshore zones for through traffic; avoid anchoring in the scheme (Rule 10).

follow.q: Does a TSS change the steering and sailing rules?
follow.a: No (Rule 10(a)), apart from the not-impede duties of small, sailing and fishing vessels.

follow.q: When may you enter the separation zone?
follow.a: When crossing, joining or leaving, in an emergency to avoid immediate danger, or to fish within it (Rule 10(e)).

verbal.q: How do you navigate in a narrow channel?
verbal.a: Keep to the starboard side as far as safe and practicable; small, sailing and fishing vessels must not impede; do not cross if it impedes; one prolonged blast at a bend; avoid anchoring (Rule 9).

follow.a: Two prolonged + one short: your starboard side. Two prolonged + two short: your port side. Agreement: P-S-P-S.

follow.q: Can a ship in a narrow channel still be the give-way vessel?
follow.a: Yes: once risk of collision exists the steering rules apply (Rule 8(f)).

verbal.q: As the stand-on vessel, when may you act, and when must you act?
verbal.a: May act by your own manoeuvre once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not acting (17(a)(ii)), after the five short blasts doubt signal. Must act when so close that collision cannot be avoided by her alone (17(b)).

follow.q: Which action should you avoid when acting under 17(a)(ii)?
follow.a: Altering to port for a power-driven vessel on your own port side (17(c)).

follow.q: Does your action relieve her of her duty?

verbal.q: Name six distress signals from Annex IV.
verbal.a: Red parachute or hand flare; orange smoke; SOS; MAYDAY; NC flags; continuous fog signal; flames on the vessel; raising and lowering arms; gun fired at one-minute intervals; DSC alert; EPIRB; SART; square flag with a ball.

follow.q: Is two all-round reds a distress signal?
follow.a: No: NUC (Rule 27(h)).

follow.q: What follows misuse of a distress signal?
follow.a: It is prohibited and an offence; cancel any false alert at once.

verbal.q: What is a proper look-out, and when may the OOW be the sole look-out?
verbal.a: Sight, hearing and all available means, to make a full appraisal of the situation and risk (Rule 5). Sole look-out only in daylight, after careful assessment, with help immediately available (STCW A-VIII/2).

follow.q: What limits AIS as a look-out aid?
follow.a: Not all vessels transmit; data may be wrong or delayed; it does not show small craft or ice.

follow.q: What distracts a look-out at night?
follow.a: Bright screens, chartwork, phone use, background shore lights; keep the bridge dark and screens dimmed.

verbal.q: Define overtaking. Who keeps clear when a yacht under sail overtakes your ship?
verbal.a: Coming up from more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam; at night only her sternlight visible. The overtaking vessel keeps clear, even a sailing vessel, because Rule 18 is subject to Rule 13.

follow.q: If in doubt whether you are overtaking?
follow.a: Assume you are (Rule 13(c)).

follow.q: Does a later change of bearing make it a crossing situation?
follow.a: No; the duty lasts until finally past and clear (Rule 13(d)).

verbal.q: Explain the order of responsibility in Rule 18.
verbal.a: Power-driven keeps clear of NUC, RAM, fishing and sailing. Sailing keeps clear of NUC, RAM and fishing. Fishing keeps clear of NUC and RAM. All except NUC and RAM avoid impeding a CBD vessel. Subject to Rules 9, 10 and 13.

follow.q: A fishing vessel and a sailing vessel converge. Who gives way?
follow.a: The sailing vessel (Rule 18(b)).
No. It is in Section II, which applies only to vessels in sight.

verbal.q: When does a head-on situation exist, and what if you are unsure?
verbal.a: Two power-driven vessels on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses: other vessel ahead or nearly ahead, masthead lights in line or nearly in line and/or both sidelights. If in doubt, assume head-on: both alter to starboard (Rule 14).

follow.a: One short blast (Rule 34(a)).

follow.q: Does Rule 14 apply to a sailing vessel?
follow.a: No; it applies between two power-driven vessels.

verbal.q: Give the arcs of the masthead light, sidelights and sternlight, and their ranges for a ship over 50 m.
verbal.a: Masthead 225 degrees, 6 nm; sidelights 112.5 degrees each, 3 nm; sternlight 135 degrees, 3 nm (Rules 21, 22).

follow.q: Why does 22.5 degrees abaft the beam matter?
follow.a: It is where masthead and sidelights end and the sternlight begins: the overtaking boundary in Rule 13.
Yellow, 135 degrees like the sternlight.

verbal.q: How do you tell a vessel at anchor from a vessel underway at night?
verbal.a: Anchor lights: two all-round whites, the forward higher, no sidelights, and the aspect never changes as you pass. Underway: masthead lights with the forward light lower, plus sidelights; deck lights on large anchored ships.

follow.q: A large ship at anchor shows deck lights. Why?
follow.a: Required at 100 m or more (Rule 30(c)).
Rapid bell for about 5 s every minute; gong aft at 100 m or more.

verbal.q: Which vessels sound one prolonged and two short blasts in restricted visibility?
verbal.a: NUC, RAM, CBD, sailing vessels, vessels engaged in fishing, and vessels towing or pushing; also fishing vessels and RAM vessels at anchor (Rule 35(c), (d)).

follow.q: What does the manned towed vessel sound?
follow.a: One prolonged + three short, immediately after the tug's signal if practicable.
Not more than 2 minutes.

verbal.q: Give the manoeuvring signals of Rule 34(a).
verbal.a: One short: I am altering my course to starboard. Two short: I am altering my course to port. Three short: I am operating astern propulsion. Only between power-driven vessels in sight.

follow.q: Can a light signal supplement them?
follow.a: Yes: one, two or three flashes of about 1 s, all-round white visible 5 nm (Rule 34(b)).
At least five short and rapid blasts (Rule 34(d)).

verbal.q: You hear a fog signal apparently forward of the beam. Nothing is on radar. What do you do?
verbal.a: Unless you have established there is no risk: reduce speed to the minimum at which you can keep your course, take all way off if necessary, navigate with extreme caution until the danger is over (Rule 19(e)). Call the Master, extra look-out, sound fog signals.

follow.q: Why might nothing show on radar?
follow.a: Small craft, wooden or GRP boats, clutter, shadow sectors, poor tuning.

follow.q: Can you judge direction from a fog signal?
follow.a: Not reliably; sound bends and fades in fog.

verbal.q: What are your duties towards a vessel constrained by her draught?
verbal.a: Unless you are NUC or RAM, avoid impeding her safe passage if circumstances admit (Rule 18(d)); act early (Rule 8(f)). She navigates with particular caution.

follow.a: Not as such. Once risk of collision exists, the steering rules apply in full.
Power-driven lights plus three all-round reds; a cylinder by day (Rule 28).

verbal.q: Define restricted visibility. Must lights be shown by day in it?
verbal.a: Visibility restricted by fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rainstorms, sandstorms or similar causes (Rule 3(l)). Yes, lights must be shown by day in restricted visibility (Rule 20(c)).

follow.q: When do you start sounding fog signals?
follow.a: When in or near an area of restricted visibility, by day or night (Rule 35).

follow.q: When would you call the Master?
follow.a: As soon as visibility drops below the limit in standing orders, or at any doubt.

verbal.q: What does 'shall not impede' mean?
verbal.a: The vessel concerned must act early to leave enough sea room for the other's safe passage (Rule 8(f)(i)). The duty continues even if risk of collision develops, and both vessels must then also follow the steering rules.

follow.a: Rules 9, 10 and 18(d).
A sailing vessel in a narrow channel must not impede a large ship that can only navigate within it.

verbal.q: What does Rule 2 mean for the OOW?
verbal.a: Following the Rules does not excuse neglect of good seamanship, and special circumstances may require departure from the Rules to avoid immediate danger.

follow.q: Give an example of departing from the Rules.
follow.a: Altering to port to avoid a collision when a starboard alteration is impossible because of shoal water, as a last resort.
No; it is about immediate danger and good seamanship, not an excuse for ignoring the steering rules early.

verbal.q: A target in fog becomes visible at 1.5 nm. Which rules apply now?
verbal.a: You are now in sight of one another: Section II applies (Rules 11 to 18) along with Section I. Determine the situation (crossing, head-on, overtaking) and act accordingly.

follow.a: Rule 19 applies again.
Manoeuvring signals under Rule 34 when you alter, plus fog signals while in or near restricted visibility.

verbal.q: When may a vessel use an inshore traffic zone?
verbal.a: Not for through traffic that can safely use the adjacent lane. Allowed: vessels under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels; any vessel bound to or from a port, offshore installation, pilot station or other place within the zone, or avoiding immediate danger (Rule 10(d)).

follow.q: What must a vessel not using a TSS do?
follow.a: Avoid it by as wide a margin as practicable (Rule 10(h)).

follow.q: Which vessels are exempted from Rule 10 when working in a TSS?
follow.a: RAM vessels maintaining safety of navigation or laying, servicing or picking up a submarine cable, to the extent necessary (Rule 10(k), (l)).

verbal.q: A trawler shows two white lights below her green over white. What is she doing?
verbal.a: Shooting her nets (Annex II). White over red: hauling. Two red: nets fast on an obstruction.

follow.q: Which vessels must show these signals?
follow.a: Trawlers of 20 m or more fishing in close proximity to other fishing vessels; optional under 20 m.
Two yellows flashing alternately every second.

verbal.q: Give the light characters of the four cardinal marks.
verbal.a: North VQ or Q continuous; East VQ(3) 5 s or Q(3) 10 s; South VQ(6)+LFl 10 s or Q(6)+LFl 15 s; West VQ(9) 10 s or Q(9) 15 s; all white.

follow.q: Why the long flash on the south mark?
follow.a: To distinguish six from three or nine.

follow.q: Which side do you pass a west cardinal?
follow.a: To the west of it.

verbal.q: What is the direction of buoyage, and how is it decided?
verbal.a: The direction in which lateral marks are read: from seaward when approaching a harbour, river or estuary; elsewhere set by the authority, generally clockwise round landmasses, and shown on the chart by an arrow where it is not obvious.

follow.q: Outbound in Region A, which side do you leave a red can?
follow.a: To starboard.

follow.q: Where do you check this for a new port?
follow.a: Chart, Sailing Directions, NP 735.

verbal.q: Define Fl, LFl, Q, VQ, Iso and Oc.
verbal.a: Fl: light shorter than dark. LFl: flash of at least 2 s. Q: 50 to 79 flashes a minute. VQ: 80 to 159 a minute. Iso: equal light and dark. Oc: light longer than dark.

follow.a: The time from the start of one sequence to the start of the next.

follow.q: How do you identify a light at night?
follow.a: Colour, rhythm and period timed over several cycles, checked against chart and List of Lights, confirmed by radar.

verbal.q: Can you fix your position from buoys?
verbal.a: Use buoys to confirm position, not as the primary fix: they may drag, sink, be off station or unlit. Fix by fixed marks, radar ranges, GNSS and other means.

follow.q: What is a virtual AIS AtoN?
follow.a: An AIS symbol transmitted for a position with no physical mark.

follow.q: How is a new wreck marked?
follow.a: Emergency wreck marking buoy (blue and yellow), racon D, navigational warnings.

verbal.q: What is the difference between IALA Regions A and B?
verbal.a: Only lateral marks differ. Region A: red to port, green to starboard. Region B: green to port, red to starboard. Shapes and all other marks are identical.

follow.a: Region B.
Region A.

verbal.q: Two sailing vessels are converging. How do you decide which gives way?
verbal.a: Different tacks: the port-tack vessel keeps clear. Same tack: windward keeps clear of leeward. A port-tack vessel unsure of the other's tack keeps clear (Rule 12).

follow.q: How is the windward side defined?
follow.a: The side opposite to that on which the mainsail is carried.

follow.q: Does Rule 12 apply if one is overtaking?
follow.a: No: Rule 13 applies to any overtaking vessel.

sounds.context: Clear visibility. A power-driven vessel in sight, ahead.
sounds.a: I am altering my course to starboard (Rule 34(a)).

follow.q: Does she have to sound it?
follow.a: Yes, when manoeuvring as authorised or required by the Rules with vessels in sight.

sounds.context: Clear visibility. A power-driven vessel in sight, ahead.
sounds.a: I am altering my course to port (Rule 34(a)).

follow.q: Should you expect her to keep altering?
follow.a: Watch her aspect and bearing; the signal reports an action, not a promise.

sounds.context: Clear visibility. A vessel in sight, close ahead.

follow.q: Does it mean she is going astern?
follow.a: Not necessarily: her engines are running astern; she may still be moving ahead.

sounds.context: Clear visibility. A crossing vessel in sight on your port bow.
sounds.a: Doubt: I fail to understand your intentions, or doubt you are taking sufficient action (Rule 34(d)).

follow.q: What should you do on hearing it?
follow.a: Reassess at once; if you are the give-way vessel take clear, substantial action now.
At least five short and rapid flashes.

sounds.context: Restricted visibility. Heard on your starboard bow every 2 minutes.
sounds.a: A power-driven vessel making way through the water (Rule 35(a)).

follow.q: In clear weather near a bend, what would one prolonged blast mean?
follow.a: A vessel approaching a bend or obscured area (Rule 34(e)).

follow.q: Your action, given she is forward of the beam?
follow.a: Rule 19(e): reduce to bare steerage way unless no risk is established; extreme caution.

sounds.context: Restricted visibility. Heard on your port bow every 2 minutes.
sounds.a: A power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way (Rule 35(b)).

follow.q: What is the gap between the two blasts?
follow.a: About 2 seconds.

sounds.context: Restricted visibility. Heard ahead every 2 minutes.
sounds.a: NUC, RAM, CBD, sailing, engaged in fishing, or towing or pushing (Rule 35(c)); or a fishing or RAM vessel at anchor (35(d)).

follow.a: Rule 19(e): reduce to bare steerage way, take all way off if necessary, extreme caution.

sounds.context: Restricted visibility. Heard just after a 'prolonged, short, short' signal from the same direction.
sounds.a: A manned vessel being towed, or the last vessel of a tow (Rule 35(e)).

follow.q: What does this tell you about the gap between the two sources?
follow.a: There is a tow between them: never pass between.

sounds.context: A narrow channel. A vessel close astern of you, in sight.
sounds.a: I intend to overtake you on your starboard side (Rule 34(c)(i)).

follow.a: One prolonged, one short, one prolonged, one short; then act to permit safe passing.

follow.q: If you are in doubt it is safe?
follow.a: At least five short and rapid blasts.

sounds.context: A narrow channel. A vessel close astern of you, in sight.
sounds.a: I intend to overtake you on your port side (Rule 34(c)(i)).

follow.q: Does your agreement relieve her of Rule 13?
follow.a: No; she still keeps out of the way.

sounds.context: A narrow channel. Reply from the vessel ahead.

follow.q: What must the overtaken vessel then do?
follow.a: Take steps to permit safe passing.

sounds.context: Restricted visibility. Heard ahead near a port approach, after a 'prolonged' signal.
sounds.q: What does this four-blast signal tell you?
sounds.a: A pilot vessel on duty, giving her identity signal (Rule 35(k)).

follow.a: White over red all-round at the masthead, plus sidelights and sternlight underway.

sounds.context: Restricted visibility. Heard close on your bow after a rapid bell.
sounds.a: A vessel at anchor warning an approaching vessel of possible collision (Rule 35(g)).

follow.a: Stop or slow, turn away if safe, navigate with extreme caution.

encounters.title: Head-on at night
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. You are a 200 m power-driven vessel at 12 knots.

options: Head-on: both vessels alter to starboard
Alter course boldly to starboard, sound one short blast, pass port to port
Alter course to port to open the CPA on her port side
Stand on: she must give way
Reduce speed slightly and call her on VHF to agree how to pass

encounters.explain: Masthead lights in line with both sidelights: a head-on situation (Rule 14). Each vessel alters to starboard and passes port to port; sound one short blast (Rule 34(a)). Check the effect until finally past and clear (Rule 8(d)). VHF agreements are no substitute for the Rules.

encounters.title: Crossing from starboard
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. You are a 200 m power-driven vessel at 12 knots.

options: Crossing: she is on your starboard side, you give way
Alter course early and boldly to starboard to pass astern of her; one short blast
Alter course to port and cross ahead of her
Stand on and sound five short blasts
Make a 5 degree alteration to starboard

encounters.explain: She shows her red sidelight on your starboard bow: you are the give-way vessel (Rule 15). Take early and substantial action (Rule 16), normally to starboard to pass astern of her, and avoid crossing ahead. A 5 degree alteration is not readily apparent (Rule 8(b)).

encounters.title: Crossing from port
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. You are a 200 m power-driven vessel at 12 knots.

options: Keep your course and speed; monitor her bearing and CPA and be ready to act under Rule 17
Alter course to port to pass astern of her
Alter course boldly to starboard now
Reduce speed to let her pass ahead

encounters.explain: She has you on her starboard side, so she must give way (Rule 15). You keep course and speed (Rule 17(a)(i)) and keep checking. You may act under 17(a)(ii) only once it is apparent she is not acting; 18 minutes out, it is too early.

encounters.title: Coming up astern
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. You are making 16 knots; the vessel ahead is slower.

options: Crossing: she is on your port bow, you stand on
Keep out of her way: alter course in good time to pass well clear, and stay clear until finally past and clear
Stand on: she is on your port side
Sound five short blasts and expect her to alter
Alter to starboard, then resume course as soon as she is abeam

encounters.explain: You can see only her sternlight, so you are more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam: you are overtaking (Rule 13). You keep out of the way until finally past and clear; being on your port bow does not make her a crossing vessel (Rule 13(d)).

encounters.title: Red light on the starboard quarter
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. You are making 10 knots. A faster ship is closing from your starboard quarter.

options: Crossing: she is on your starboard side, you give way
Stand on: keep your course and speed and monitor; she must keep out of the way
Alter course to starboard to pass astern of her
Alter course to port to open the distance
Reduce speed to let her cross ahead

encounters.explain: She is about 53 degrees abaft your beam, so she is overtaking (Rule 13), even though you can see her red sidelight. You are the stand-on vessel (Rule 17). Altering to starboard would turn you towards her.

encounters.title: Give-way vessel not acting
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. She has made no alteration in the last 10 minutes and does not answer VHF.

options: Crossing: you stand on, and she is not taking action
Sound at least five short and rapid blasts; if she still does not act, take action yourself: a bold alteration to starboard or a large speed reduction, never to port
Alter course to port to pass astern of her
Keep your course and speed whatever happens until she acts
Sound one prolonged blast and keep going

encounters.explain: Sound the doubt signal (Rule 34(d)), call the Master, then act under Rule 17(a)(ii). Rule 17(c): do not alter to port for a vessel on your own port side. If collision can no longer be avoided by her alone, you must act (Rule 17(b)).

encounters.title: Two red lights crossing from port
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. You are a 200 m power-driven vessel at 12 knots.

options: She is not under command: you keep out of her way
Crossing: you stand on, she is on your port side
She is restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Keep out of her way: reduce speed early and substantially, or stop, so she passes clear ahead
Stand on: she is on your port side
Alter to starboard and cross ahead of her
Sound five short blasts and wait for her to alter

encounters.explain: Two all-round reds with a sidelight and no masthead lights: not under command, making way (Rule 27(a)). A power-driven vessel keeps out of her way whichever side she is on (Rule 18(a)). Slowing or stopping (Rule 8(e)) lets her pass ahead; turning to cross ahead of a vessel that cannot manoeuvre is poor seamanship.

encounters.title: Trawler on the starboard bow
encounters.brief: Coastal waters at night, fishing boats about. You are a 200 m power-driven vessel at 12 knots.

options: She is trawling: you keep out of her way
A power-driven vessel crossing: you stand on
Alter course early and boldly to starboard to pass well astern of her and her gear
Alter course to port and pass ahead of her
Stand on: she is slow and will clear
Pass close astern of her: her trawl is alongside

encounters.explain: Green over white with a red sidelight: trawling, making way, showing her port side (Rule 26(b)). You keep out of her way (Rule 18(a)), and she is on your starboard side anyway. Give her a wide berth astern: a trawl can be a long way behind her.

encounters.title: Yacht closing from the port quarter
encounters.brief: Clear night. You are a tug, not towing, making 5 knots. A yacht under sail is closing from your port quarter.

options: She is overtaking you, so she keeps out of the way
She is a sailing vessel, so you keep out of her way
Stand on: keep your course and speed and monitor; be ready to act under Rule 17 if she does not keep clear
Alter to starboard to give way to the sailing vessel
Stop engines to let her pass
Alter to port across her bow

encounters.explain: She is about 47 degrees abaft your port beam, so she is overtaking (Rule 13). Rule 18 starts 'except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 otherwise require', so the overtaking sailing vessel keeps clear and you stand on (Rule 17).

encounters.title: Nearly head-on
encounters.brief: Open sea, clear night. You are a 200 m power-driven vessel at 12 knots.

options: Treat it as head-on: if in doubt, assume it is
Alter course boldly to starboard and sound one short blast
Alter course to port to pass starboard to starboard
Stand on: she is showing her red light
Reduce speed slightly and wait to see what she does

encounters.explain: She is nearly ahead with her masthead lights nearly in line (Rule 14(b)). If in any doubt, assume a head-on situation and alter to starboard (Rule 14(c)). Altering to port for a vessel fine on your starboard bow risks turning across her bow.

encounters.title: Fog: target on the starboard bow
encounters.brief: Dense fog, visibility 0.3 nm. Fog signals sounding, Master informed. Radar contact only.

options: Restricted visibility: no stand-on or give-way, Rule 19 applies
Alter course boldly to starboard and/or reduce speed, in ample time
Alter course to port to pass ahead of her
Stand on: she is crossing from starboard
Make small alterations to port to open the CPA

encounters.explain: The vessels are not in sight, so Section II does not apply (Rule 11). Under Rule 19(d), act in ample time and avoid altering to port for a vessel forward of the beam. A bold starboard alteration, a speed reduction, or both are correct.

encounters.title: Fog: target on the port bow
encounters.brief: Dense fog, visibility 0.3 nm. Radar contact only.

options: Restricted visibility: Rule 19, no stand-on vessel
Alter course boldly to starboard and/or reduce speed; avoid altering to port
Alter course to port to pass astern of her
Keep your course and speed: you are the stand-on vessel
Increase speed to cross ahead of her

encounters.explain: Rule 19(d)(i): avoid altering to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than one being overtaken. Make an early, bold starboard alteration, reduce speed, or both. There is no 'stand-on vessel' in restricted visibility.

encounters.title: Fog: target on the starboard quarter
encounters.brief: Dense fog, visibility 0.3 nm. You are making 10 knots. Radar contact only, closing from astern.

options: Restricted visibility: Rule 19, the target is abaft your starboard beam
She is overtaking you, so you stand on
If action is needed, alter course to port, away from her; avoid altering to starboard towards her
Alter course to starboard to pass astern of her
Reduce speed sharply to let her pass
Keep your course and speed: she is overtaking

encounters.explain: Rule 13 is in Section II, so it does not apply when not in sight: there is no overtaking or stand-on vessel. Rule 19(d)(ii): avoid altering towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam, so alter to port, away from her. Slowing down would only let her close faster.

encounters.title: Fog: overtaking a slower target
encounters.brief: Dense fog, visibility 0.3 nm. You are making 14 knots. Radar contact only, slower and on a similar course.

options: Restricted visibility: Rule 19, and you are overtaking her
No action needed: she is slower
Alter course to port to pass her on your starboard side; Rule 19(d)(i) allows this for a vessel being overtaken
Alter course to starboard, towards her
Sound five short blasts and stand on

encounters.explain: You are coming up from astern, so she is a vessel being overtaken. Rule 19(d)(i) exempts this case from 'avoid altering to port'. With her fine on your starboard bow, a port alteration opens the CPA quickest. Reduce speed too if needed.

encounters.title: Fog: target on the port quarter
encounters.brief: Dense fog, visibility 0.3 nm. You are making 10 knots. Radar contact only, closing from astern.

options: Restricted visibility: Rule 19, the target is abaft your port beam
She is overtaking you, so you stand on
If action is needed, alter course to starboard, away from her; avoid altering to port towards her
Keep your course and speed: she is overtaking

encounters.explain: Rule 19(d)(ii): avoid altering towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam. She is abaft your port beam, so a starboard alteration takes you away from her.

encounters.title: Fog signal heard ahead
encounters.brief: Dense fog, visibility under 0.2 nm. You hear this signal apparently fine on your starboard bow. Nothing shows on either radar.

options: A vessel such as NUC, RAM, CBD, sailing, fishing or towing, forward of the beam
Reduce to the minimum speed at which you can keep your course, take all way off if necessary, navigate with extreme caution; call the Master
Alter course boldly to port, away from the sound
Keep your speed: nothing is on radar

encounters.explain: Rule 19(e): on hearing a fog signal apparently forward of the beam, unless you have established there is no risk, reduce to bare steerage way, take all way off if necessary, and navigate with extreme caution. Small craft may not show on radar, and sound direction in fog is unreliable.

encounters.title: Crossing a TSS lane
encounters.brief: You are following the north-east-bound lane of a TSS at 14 knots. She is crossing the lane at right angles.

options: Crossing: she is on your starboard side, you give way
She must keep clear: vessels in the lane have right of way
Give way: alter to starboard or reduce speed in good time, staying within the lane
Stand on: crossing vessels must keep clear of lane traffic
Alter to port into the separation zone
Sound five short blasts and stand on

encounters.explain: A TSS does not relieve any vessel of her obligations under the other Rules (Rule 10(a)). Only vessels under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels have a duty not to impede lane traffic. This is a normal Rule 15 crossing and you give way. Keep out of the separation zone (Rule 10(b), (e)).

encounters.title: Small craft crossing a channel
encounters.brief: You are a 180 m ship in a narrow channel at 8 knots and can navigate safely only within it. A motor boat of about 15 m is crossing from starboard.

options: She must not impede you, but if risk of collision develops the steering rules still apply
She has right of way because she is on your starboard side, whatever the channel
You stand on: small vessels always give way
Sound at least five short and rapid blasts if in doubt of her intentions; if risk of collision still develops, reduce speed or stop as needed
Hold your course and speed: she must keep clear
Alter hard to port out of the channel
Increase speed to pass ahead of her

encounters.explain: Rule 9(b) and (d): she must not impede you or cross if that impedes you, and you may sound the doubt signal (Rule 34(d)). Rule 8(f)(iii): once risk of collision exists, the vessel whose passage is not to be impeded must still follow the steering rules. In a channel, reducing speed or stopping is usually the safe option.
